events.text: Old Ma the paper-maker is throwing out a torn sheet of mulberry paper as wide as a door. You ask for it. Ma squints at you. 'And what would a sprout do with that?' 'Fly it,' you say. Ma laughs for a long time, then fetches bamboo.

choices.text: Ask for a carp, the fish that climbs the waterfall

effects.log: Ma paints scales on it with soot and a red eye with cinnabar. It takes six evenings. On the seventh it flies over the threshing floor and every dog in the village barks at the sky.

choices.text: Ask for a dragon, the biggest thing there is

effects.log: The dragon is too heavy and flies like a dizzy duck. Ma says the paper knew better than you. You fly it anyway, very low, and are completely happy.

choices.text: Help Ma first, then decide

effects.log: You spend the week sorting paper scraps by thickness. By the end you can tell good paper from bad with your eyes shut, and Ma builds you a carp without being asked.

events.text: A wind comes off the mountain in the third month, the kind that pulls washing off the lines. The kite strains at its string like a live fish. Half the children in the village are watching you.

choices.text: Let out all the string

ok.log: The kite climbs until it is a red dot above the temple roof. A passing peddler stops his cart to look. For one afternoon you own the sky.

fail.log: The string bites your palms and snaps. The kite goes over the hill like a fish escaping a net. You chase it until dark and come home with nothing but the reel.

choices.text: Let the smallest child hold the reel

effects.log: The little one shrieks with joy and nearly lets go twice. You keep a hand on the string behind, where nobody sees. The child tells everyone, for a year, about flying it alone.

choices.text: Reel it in. This wind is too greedy

effects.log: You bring it down safe while two other kites end up in the river. Ma, hearing of it, says: 'A flier who knows when to land. Rare.'

events.text: Up on the roof of the hill temple, wedged behind a clay roof-fish, something red and tattered flaps in the wind. The novice who sweeps the roof says a kite has been stuck there for years. 'A fish that wanted to be a dragon,' he says.

choices.text: Climb up and bring it home

effects.log: The bamboo has gone grey and the red has gone pink, but the soot scales are still there. You carry it to Ma, who is very old now, and sits with it across both knees for a long while without speaking.

choices.text: Leave it there. It found its waterfall

effects.log: You bow to the roof. The novice thinks you are strange. The kite stays, and every time you pass the temple you look up, and it is still climbing.

choices.text: Build a new kite with Ma, and fly it from the temple steps

effects.log: Your hands know the bamboo now. Ma only points. The new carp flies higher than any kite the village has seen, right over the old one on the roof, as if to say hello.

events.text: In the corner of the teahouse an old storyteller slaps a wooden block on the table and the room goes quiet. Today it is the Nine Swords of the Southern Peak. You cannot afford tea. You crouch under the window outside and listen.

choices.text: Listen until the very end

effects.log: The swordsman wins in the last breath. You walk home with your arms swinging an invisible sword, and fall in a ditch, and do not care.

choices.text: Sneak in and sit under a table

effects.log: A teahouse boy finds you and is about to throw you out. The storyteller, without pausing the tale, points the fan at the empty stool by the door. You may stay. You do not breathe for an hour.

choices.text: Run home and act it out for the chickens

effects.log: The chickens are a poor audience. But you remember nearly every line, and say them to the yard until your voice cracks.

events.text: The storyteller has noticed you. 'You. Window child. What happened to the third sword?' Everyone in the teahouse turns around. It is a test. You know the answer. You also know the storyteller changed it last week.

choices.text: Give the old ending, word for word

effects.log: Word for word, down to the slap of the block, which you make with your palm on the sill. The teahouse laughs and claps. The storyteller nods once, like a teacher.

choices.text: Give the new ending, and say why it is better

effects.log: 'Because in the new one the third sword is never drawn.' The room goes quiet. The storyteller looks at you for a long time. 'Come in. Sit. You will pour the tea.'

choices.text: Make up a fourth ending on the spot

effects.log: It is a bad ending with a flying ox in it. The teahouse howls. The storyteller laughs so hard the fan falls on the floor, then picks it up and says: 'Again. Slower. Without the ox.'

events.text: The storyteller's voice is going. In the middle of the Battle at Red Cliff Gorge it cracks and does not come back. Forty people are waiting. The old one looks at you, coughs, and slides the wooden block across the table.

choices.text: Take the block and finish the tale

effects.log: Your voice shakes for the first ten lines and then it does not. When the gorge burns, a merchant drops his cup. When it ends, nobody claps for a moment, and then everybody does.

choices.text: Finish it together: you speak, the old one slaps the block

effects.log: You have heard this tale forty times. The block comes down exactly where you pause, every time, as if you had practised. Afterwards the storyteller says you did.

choices.text: Pour tea and ask the room to come back tomorrow

effects.log: Nobody minds. They leave coins anyway. The storyteller gets the voice back in a month, and from then on always tells the room you were the one who saved the evening.

events.text: In the mud at the edge of the lotus pond there is a stone that blinks. It is a turtle no bigger than your palm, with a crack in its shell shaped like a lightning bolt.

choices.text: Carry it home in your shirt

effects.log: You keep it in a water jar and name it General. General eats one grain of rice in three days and looks at you as if you are the one being kept.

choices.text: Leave it where it is, but visit every day

effects.log: Every day for a month you crouch by the pond. On the thirtieth day it does not hide its head. You are very proud of this.

choices.text: Show it to everyone

effects.log: Everyone has seen a turtle before. You explain that this one is different. The miller's child agrees, and you are friends from that moment.

events.text: Winter. The turtle is gone. The water jar is empty, the pond is grey ice, and nobody has seen it.

choices.text: Search the whole village

effects.log: You look under every step and in every jar. A neighbour tells you turtles sleep in the mud all winter. You do not believe it until spring.

choices.text: Ask the old fisherman

effects.log: 'Under the mud, sleeping, breathing about once a day,' he says. 'Wiser than us.' You practise breathing once a minute, which is very hard, and fall asleep.

choices.text: Leave a grain of rice at the pond every morning

effects.log: The ice keeps the rice. The magpies get it. You keep leaving it anyway, all winter, because a promise to a turtle is still a promise.

events.text: Spring. A turtle the size of a rice bowl climbs out of the mud and sits on your foot. There is a lightning bolt on its shell. It is much bigger now. So are you.

choices.text: Carry it to the big river and let it go

effects.log: It sits on the bank for a long moment, looking back, the way old men look at a village they are leaving. Then it goes. Turtles live a hundred years. Somewhere it is still swimming.

choices.text: Keep it in the pond where it belongs

effects.log: General becomes the village's turtle. Children are told it is a thousand years old and can grant wishes. You do not correct this.

choices.text: Sit and breathe with it in the sun

effects.log: It closes its eyes. You close yours. Your breath slows to match something very old and very calm. When you open your eyes the shadows have moved an hour.

events.text: In the autumn every child in the lane keeps a fighting cricket in a clay pot. You catch yours in the woodpile: black, fat, with a chirp like a creaking door. You name it Iron-Jaw.

choices.text: Feed it the best: millet and cucumber

effects.log: You give it the cucumber off your own bowl. Iron-Jaw grows shiny and rude. It bites your finger. You are delighted.

choices.text: Train it with a straw, every evening

effects.log: You tickle its feelers with a rice straw until it rushes the straw like a tiger. You fall asleep most nights with your chin on the pot.

choices.text: Let it go. It wanted to sing, not fight

effects.log: It sings in the woodpile all autumn. The other children think you are soft. You fall asleep every night to your own cricket, free.

events.text: Every autumn since, there has been a new Iron-Jaw from the same woodpile. This year, at the lane tournament, the rich family's child has brought a champion called Jade Thunder, and a servant to hold an umbrella over its pot.

choices.text: Put this year's Iron-Jaw in the ring

ok.log: Iron-Jaw grabs Jade Thunder by the leg and tips it over. The lane erupts. The rich child cries, and you, surprising yourself, offer a sesame cake.

fail.log: Jade Thunder chirps once and Iron-Jaw runs out of the pot and across the lane. The crowd laughs. You catch it and tell it that it was very brave, which it was not.

choices.text: Bring a singer instead of a fighter

effects.log: You bring a woodpile cricket in your cupped hands and let it sing at the ring. It outsings Jade Thunder, which only fights. The little ones declare a new contest, for singing, and you win it.

choices.text: Stay out: the cricket is tired

effects.log: The rich child crows victory. Your cricket sings all evening anyway. You decide that a champion who sings is better than one who wins.

choices.text: Sell your cricket to the rich child for twenty coppers

effects.log: Twenty coppers buys a great many sesame cakes. That night the lane is very quiet, and you find you cannot finish the last cake.

events.text: The first frost. The singing has stopped. In the morning the cricket lies on its back, small and light, as if it was only ever made of paper.

choices.text: Bury it under the plum tree

effects.log: You dig with a spoon. You put in a grain of millet for the road. A friend from the lane comes and stands with you and does not say anything, which is exactly right.

choices.text: Ask why crickets only live one autumn

effects.log: An old aunt says: 'So that they sing all of it.' You think about this for years. You think about it still, sometimes, when a good season is ending.

choices.text: Keep the empty pot on the windowsill

effects.log: Next autumn, without being put there, a cricket climbs into the empty pot and sings. It is not the same one. You let it stay anyway.

events.arc: The Voice in the Dry Well
events.text: Behind the old granary is a dry well nobody uses. The children dare each other to shout into it. When you shout, the well answers, a moment late, in a deep and grumpy voice: 'Some of us are trying to sleep.'

choices.text: Shout back: Who are you?

effects.log: 'A frog,' says the well. 'A large and important frog.' You are nearly sure frogs do not talk. Nearly.

choices.text: Run home very fast

effects.log: You run so fast your shoe stays behind. The next morning it is sitting on your doorstep, neatly, with a dried date inside it.

choices.text: Drop a rice ball down as an apology

effects.log: There is a pause, then chewing. 'Better,' says the well. 'Less salt next time.'

events.arc: The Voice in the Dry Well
events.text: You follow a crack in the granary wall and find the secret: a clay pipe runs from the well into the cellar of the cobbler's shop next door. In the cellar, on a straw mat, an old man with one ear sits breathing very slowly.

choices.text: Ask the old man to teach you to breathe like that

effects.log: He opens one eye. 'Like a frog?' He shows you: in through the nose for eight, hold for eight, out for eight. You go purple. He laughs, the same grumpy laugh as the well.

choices.text: Promise to keep the secret

effects.log: He nods. 'Then you can come down when it rains.' You do, all season, and he tells you about places you have never heard of, and once, with no expression at all, about a war.

choices.text: Tell the other children

effects.log: By evening there are nine children in the cellar. The old man sighs the longest sigh you have ever heard and teaches all nine of you to sit still. Seven fail.

events.arc: The Voice in the Dry Well
events.text: The cobbler says the old man has gone. On the straw mat in the cellar is a pair of worn straw sandals, a faded sword tassel, and a note in a shaky hand: For the child who comes down when it rains.

choices.text: Tie the sword tassel to your belt

effects.log: It is faded blue silk, very old. A traveller once sees it on your belt, goes white, and asks where you got it. You do not tell. The traveller bows to you before leaving.

choices.text: Keep breathing the frog way, every night

effects.log: Eight, eight, eight. One night you notice your breath has stopped being a count and become a tide. You think the old man would grunt at that, approvingly.

choices.text: Drop one last rice ball down the well

effects.log: It lands with a soft pat. Nothing answers. Then, a moment late, very faint, a frog croaks. It is just a frog. You are almost sure.

events.arc: The War of the Two Lanes
events.text: Heavy snow overnight. By breakfast the children of East Lane have built a wall of snow across the alley and declared themselves a kingdom. The children of West Lane, including you, are not having it.

choices.text: Build a bigger wall

effects.log: By noon West Lane has a fortress with a watchtower made of a rain barrel. The two kingdoms glare at each other across six steps of trampled snow.

choices.text: Make a hundred snowballs and attack

effects.log: It is the shortest war in history. West Lane wins. East Lane wants a rematch. Everyone is soaked to the knees and grinning.

choices.text: Send an envoy with a roasted chestnut

effects.log: You walk across with a white rag on a stick and a hot chestnut. The East Lane king accepts the chestnut and then hits you with a snowball. Diplomacy, you learn, is complicated.

events.arc: The War of the Two Lanes
events.text: The next winter the war resumes. This time East Lane has a secret weapon: the blacksmith's tall child, who throws like a catapult. West Lane is losing. Everyone looks at you.

choices.text: Lead a charge around the back, through the pigsty

ok.log: You come out of the pigsty, filthy and victorious, behind the East Lane wall. The catapult surrenders. You smell terrible for three days and are a hero for thirty.

fail.log: The pig objects. You arrive behind the wall covered in mud and pig, and East Lane laughs too hard to fight. Somehow this counts as a draw.

choices.text: Recruit the catapult to your side

effects.log: You offer the blacksmith's child your best hat. The catapult defects. East Lane calls it treason. You call it strategy, a word you learned from a storyteller.

choices.text: Call a truce and build one big fortress together

effects.log: The great snow fortress of both lanes has two towers and a tunnel. Grown-ups come out to look at it. The headman says it is the best thing anyone has built all year.

events.arc: The War of the Two Lanes
events.text: Snow again. From the window you watch the little ones of both lanes building walls across the alley. They are doing it all wrong. One of them, very small, is crying because the East Lane wall fell over.

choices.text: Go out and show them how to pack snow

effects.log: You show them the trick: wet the inside, pack it with the flat of the hand. Their wall stands. They make you their general. You retire after one battle, undefeated.

choices.text: Stay inside. It is their war now

effects.log: You watch them fight it badly and happily. Something in your chest aches a little, in a good way. You are not a child of the lanes any more. Nearly.

choices.text: Lead the old veterans of both lanes in one last battle

effects.log: The old kingdoms, half of them taller than their parents now, against the little ones. You lose on purpose. It is the most fun anyone has had in years.

events.text: You have watched the school children through the fence. With a stick of charcoal you copy the character for 'person' onto the white wall of the rice merchant's shop. Then 'big'. Then 'heaven'.

choices.text: Keep going until the wall is full

effects.log: By evening the wall says, more or less, 'person big heaven big person heaven'. The rice merchant comes out and stares at it for a very long time.

choices.text: Wipe it off before anyone sees

effects.log: You wipe it with your sleeve and your sleeve is ruined. But the characters are in your head now, where no sleeve can reach.

choices.text: Sign it with a drawing of yourself

effects.log: You do not know how to write your name, so you draw yourself. The rice merchant knows exactly who did it.

events.text: The rice merchant catches you by the collar. Behind the merchant, the wall has been washed, except for one character, 'heaven', which has been carefully left. 'You wrote that one upside down,' the merchant says. 'Again. Correctly.'

choices.text: Write it correctly

effects.log: It takes you nine tries. On the tenth the merchant grunts. 'Every evening, after I close. One character. Wash it off when you go.' It is the beginning of your education.

choices.text: Ask why the merchant cares

effects.log: 'Because my father wrote on walls too, and nobody taught him.' The merchant says it to the wall, not to you. Then hands you the charcoal.

choices.text: Run away

effects.log: You run. The next evening there is a new character on the wall, in a clean grown-up hand: 'come back'. You go back.

events.text: The rice merchant's old shop sign cracked in the rains. A new board, planed and pale, leans against the wall. The merchant holds out a brush, a real one, with a pot of real ink.

choices.text: Write the sign: Honest Rice

effects.log: Your hand does not shake. People stop in the street to watch. The sign hangs for twenty years, and the merchant tells every customer who wrote it.

choices.text: Say the merchant should write it

effects.log: 'My hand is old.' 'Then we write it together.' Your hand on the brush, the old hand over yours. The characters come out a little crooked, and perfect.

choices.text: Write it, and add one tiny 'heaven' in the corner

effects.log: Nobody notices but the merchant, who laughs out loud for the first time you can remember.

events.text: A yellow dog with three legs has been sleeping under the bridge. It flinches when anyone comes near. The butcher throws stones at it. It is thin enough to count its ribs.

choices.text: Leave half your rice by the bridge every day

effects.log: For eleven days it waits until you are gone. On the twelfth day it eats while you are still there. On the twentieth it follows you home, hopping, at a careful distance.

choices.text: Stand between it and the butcher's stones

effects.log: The butcher stops, startled, a stone in hand. 'It steals.' 'It is hungry,' you say. The butcher looks at the dog, and at you, and goes back inside.

choices.text: Name it Lucky, as a joke

effects.log: Three legs, no home, no luck. Lucky. You say it to the dog and it lifts its head. It thinks it is a good name. Maybe it is.

events.text: A boar comes down from the hills into the gardens at dusk, snorting, and the children scatter. Lucky, who has never barked in its life, plants itself in front of you on three legs and barks like thunder.

choices.text: Pull Lucky back and run for the gate

effects.log: You drag Lucky by the scruff. The boar tears up the turnips instead of you. The village decides the dog is brave. Nobody throws stones at it again.

choices.text: Bang a pot and shout with the dog

effects.log: Pot and bark together. The boar decides the turnips next door are better. That night Lucky is allowed to sleep inside, by the stove, for the first time.

choices.text: Climb the wall and call for the grown-ups

effects.log: The grown-ups come with poles and torches. Lucky stands guard at the bottom of the wall the whole time, growling, not moving an inch.

events.text: Lucky is old now, grey around the muzzle, and sleeps most of the day in the sun by the door. This morning it does not get up when you come out. It only thumps its tail twice on the ground.

choices.text: Sit with it in the sun all day

effects.log: You sit there until the shadows cross the yard. Lucky's breathing gets slower and quieter, and then it is just the sun. It was a very good dog.

choices.text: Carry it to the bridge where you met

effects.log: It is heavy now. You lay it in the grass by the water. Its nose works at the old smells for a long time, and then it sighs, contented, home.

choices.text: Bury it under the gate, so it can guard

effects.log: The whole lane comes. Even the butcher, who brings a bone and puts it in the grave without a word. Children say for years that the gate is guarded by a dog no one can see.

events.arc: The Lost Child of the Lantern Festival
events.text: Lantern Festival. The streets are rivers of light and people. Under a rabbit lantern a much smaller child called Little Bean is standing perfectly still, holding a half-eaten sugar figure, about to cry. Bean knows only that Mother has a blue scarf. Somewhere far off in the noise, someone is shouting a name that might be 'Bean'.

choices.text: Push through the crowd toward the voice

ok.log: You come out of the crush face to face with a blue scarf. The mother snatches Bean up and cries into the child's hair and then, embarrassingly, into yours.

fail.log: The crowd sweeps you down a side street. It takes an hour, but you find the blue scarf by the bridge, and Little Bean falls asleep on your back on the way.

choices.text: Lift Bean onto your shoulders like a lighthouse

effects.log: Bean, up high, stops being frightened and starts waving the sugar figure and shouting. A blue scarf comes running. Bean's father, who sells noodles, says you will never pay for noodles again.

choices.text: Stay still under the rabbit lantern

effects.log: The storytellers always say: the lost should stay still. You do, holding the small sticky hand. It works. The mother comes back to the rabbit lantern within the hour, frantic, then weeping.

events.arc: The Lost Child of the Lantern Festival
events.text: A year on, the noodle seller's family finds you in the market: Little Bean, the blue scarf, the father with a bowl of noodles held out in both hands like an offering. Bean has decided you are an elder sibling now, and that is that.

choices.text: Accept the noodles, and the sibling

effects.log: You eat the noodles with Bean watching every mouthful. From then on Bean follows you around the market like a duckling, and you find you do not mind at all.

choices.text: Say it was nothing

effects.log: 'It was not nothing,' says the blue scarf, very firmly, and the father nods, and Bean, not understanding, nods hardest of all.

choices.text: Teach Bean the way home from the market

effects.log: Left at the well, right at the rice merchant, past the temple. You walk it together three times. Bean recites it all the way, very loud, like a sutra.

events.arc: The Lost Child of the Lantern Festival
events.text: Every Lantern Festival since, a child has come to your door with a bowl of sweet dumplings. This year Little Bean is not so little, and has brought a lantern made for you, shaped very badly like a carp.

choices.text: Take Bean to the festival this year

effects.log: This time it is Bean holding your hand, so as not to lose you, very seriously. You let yourself be led. It is a very good festival.

choices.text: Teach Bean what to do if ever lost again

effects.log: Stand still. Look for a lantern. Shout your street, your name, the blue scarf. Bean repeats it like a sutra. You hope it is never needed.

choices.text: Hang the crooked lantern over your door

effects.log: It is the ugliest lantern in the street. The neighbours tease you all week. You leave it up until it falls apart in the summer rains.

events.arc: The Board Under the Locust Tree
events.text: Under the locust tree at the crossroads an old man plays go against himself every afternoon, black and white, muttering at both sides. When you crouch to watch, he slides the bowl of black stones toward you without looking up.

choices.text: Play, and lose quickly

effects.log: You lose in forty moves. He nods. 'Again.' You lose in thirty-eight. He seems pleased by this, which makes no sense to you at all.

choices.text: Ask him to teach you the rules first

effects.log: 'The rules take a minute,' he says. 'The game takes a life.' The minute takes the whole afternoon. You go home seeing grids on the rice paddies.

choices.text: Put your stone in the middle, where it looks strongest

effects.log: He laughs so hard he has to hold the tree. 'The middle is where everybody wants to be,' he says. 'So it is where everybody fights.' You lose. You remember.

events.arc: The Board Under the Locust Tree
events.text: A hundred games. You have lost every one. Today, in the corner of the board, you see something: if you give up these six stones, his whole wall falls. It feels like cheating. It feels like the sky opening.

choices.text: Sacrifice the six stones

effects.log: His hand stops over the bowl. He looks at the board for a long time, and then at you. 'Who taught you that?' 'You did. A hundred times.' You win by half a point.

choices.text: Keep your stones; you worked hard for them

effects.log: You keep them and lose by twenty. On the way home you realise what you should have done, and lie awake furious and delighted.

choices.text: Show him the move instead of playing it

effects.log: You point. He grunts. 'Play it, then.' 'It is not fair to beat you with your own lesson.' He looks at you oddly. 'That is the only way anyone has ever beaten anyone.'

events.arc: The Board Under the Locust Tree
events.text: The old man is not under the locust tree. His neighbour brings you the board, wrapped in a quilted cloth, and a bowl of black stones and a bowl of white. 'Said you would know what to do with them.'

choices.text: Play under the locust tree, against yourself

effects.log: Black, white, muttering at both sides. After a week a small child crouches to watch. You slide the bowl of black stones toward the child, without looking up.

choices.text: Keep the board at home, and study the old games

effects.log: In the drawer under the board are his records: forty years of games, in tiny characters. In the last ten pages, game after game is marked with your name.

choices.text: Bring the board to the teahouse and find opponents

effects.log: You lose to a cloth merchant, beat a monk, lose to a monk, and become the person the teahouse sends challengers to. The old man would grunt at that.

events.arc: The King of the Mill Pond
events.text: Everyone knows about the great carp in the mill pond. It is older than the mill. It is as long as a door. It ate a duck once. Nobody has ever caught it, and you, with a willow rod and a bent pin, intend to.

choices.text: Fish at dawn, when the miller says it feeds

effects.log: You catch three minnows and a cold. At the very end, a swirl in the middle of the pond, wide as a cartwheel, as if something enormous is laughing.

choices.text: Bait the pin with a sweet dumpling

effects.log: Something takes the dumpling, pin and all, so gently you never feel it. The miller laughs at you. 'It likes you. It never takes mine.'

choices.text: Sit and watch the water instead

effects.log: You watch all afternoon. Just before dusk you see it: gold and black, slow as a cloud, passing under the mill wheel. It looks at you. You forget to breathe.

events.arc: The King of the Mill Pond
events.text: Drought. The mill pond shrinks to a muddy bowl. Boys from the next village come with nets and a wagon, laughing, to take the great carp to sell in the town. It lies in the last deep water, barely moving.

choices.text: Stand in the mud in front of it and refuse to move

effects.log: They could shove you aside. They do not. The miller comes out with a pole and stands beside you, and after that nobody is shoving anyone.

choices.text: Run for the miller and the headman

effects.log: The headman declares the carp the property of the village, which was not true before but is now. The net boys go home grumbling.

choices.text: Carry buckets from the well all night to deepen the water

effects.log: Forty trips. Your arms shake. By dawn half the village children are carrying buckets with you, and the carp has water enough to wait for rain.

events.arc: The King of the Mill Pond
events.text: The rains come back. The mill pond fills. One morning you take your willow rod down, and the great carp rises under the bank, right at your feet, and stays there, gold and black, looking at you.

choices.text: Drop your line in front of it

effects.log: It takes the bait. It is on your line, enormous, and for one long moment it simply lets you hold it. Then it shakes the pin out of its lip as easily as a sneeze, and sinks away. You caught it. Nobody else ever has.

choices.text: Put the rod down and just look back

effects.log: You and the carp, for a long time. Then it goes down into the green and you never see it again. The pond feels full, even when you cannot see it.

choices.text: Feed it the whole of your lunch

effects.log: It eats like a king. The miller says that carp will outlive the mill, and the miller, and maybe you. You find you like that idea very much.

events.text: The scarecrow in the millet field is a sad thing in a sack. You have heard the storytellers. You decide it should be a sword saint instead.

choices.text: Give it a stick sword and a fierce painted face

effects.log: Its eyebrows are enormous. Its stick sword points at the mountains. The sparrows are unimpressed. The farmer's wife laughs until she has to sit down.

choices.text: Dress it in your own old jacket

effects.log: It looks like you, a bit, from far off. A neighbour waves at it in the dusk and asks it why it is not home for dinner.

choices.text: Give it a name: Sword Saint of the Millet

effects.log: You announce the name to the field. A crow lands on its head. You decide the crow is its disciple.

events.text: A real martial artist, dusty from the road, stops at the edge of the millet field and stares at the scarecrow for a long time. Then the stranger bows to it, very gravely, and asks who taught it that stance.

choices.text: Say: I did

effects.log: The stranger looks at you, then at the scarecrow's crooked stick. 'The arm is wrong.' And for an hour, on the field's edge, you are taught how to hold a sword properly, by someone who knows.

choices.text: Say: the Sword Saint is meditating and cannot be disturbed

effects.log: The stranger laughs, a real laugh, and sits down by the field to share a rice cake with you and the scarecrow. The scarecrow does not eat.

choices.text: Challenge the stranger on the scarecrow's behalf

effects.log: You lose instantly, to a flick of a finger. The stranger is delighted. 'A good disciple defends the master's name. Hold your stick like this, little one.'

events.text: After a storm the scarecrow lies in the millet with its sack head split. The farmer says it is time for a new one. The crow sits on the fence, looking at you.

choices.text: Rebuild it exactly as it was

effects.log: Same eyebrows, same stick, same stance. Except the arm is right now. Travellers still bow to it, years later, not knowing why.

choices.text: Practise the stance it taught you, there, in the field

effects.log: The stranger's stance, every morning beside the empty pole, until the crow stops flying away. Your arm is right too.

choices.text: Let the field have it, and keep the stick

effects.log: You keep the stick sword. It is just a stick. You keep it for a very long time.

events.text: Granny Shen, who gathers herbs on the hill, has a bad knee this spring. She stands at the bottom of the slope with her empty basket, looking at it as if it had insulted her.

choices.text: Offer to climb for her

effects.log: She tells you what to look for: leaves like a cat's ear, a root that smells of licorice. You come back with a basket of nettles and one right root. She is pleased about the root.

choices.text: Offer to carry her up on your back

effects.log: You make it ten steps. She laughs so much you both sit down. You end up her eyes and legs, and she ends up teaching you, both by accident.

choices.text: Fetch your friends to help

effects.log: Four children and one bad knee climb the hill. The children learn nothing and pick everything. Granny Shen sorts it on her doorstep, grumbling happily.

events.text: The miller's goat has eaten something on the hill and lies on its side, groaning. The miller is shouting for the butcher. Granny Shen is away at her sister's.

choices.text: Find the root that settles a belly

ok.log: Licorice smell, cat's ear leaves. You chew it soft and feed it to the goat. By evening the goat is standing and trying to eat your sleeve. The miller gives you a cheese.

fail.log: You bring the wrong root. The goat eats it anyway, and the goat, being a goat, gets better on its own by morning. Granny Shen, told of it, sighs.

choices.text: Run to fetch Granny Shen from her sister's

effects.log: It is two hours there and back. She rides back on the miller's cart, scolding everyone, and the goat lives.

choices.text: Sit with the goat and keep it calm

effects.log: You hold its head and talk to it all afternoon. Whether it is the talking or the goat's own stubbornness, it is up by dark.

events.text: Granny Shen gives you a bundle wrapped in oilcloth: a book of herbs, hand-copied, with pressed leaves between the pages. 'My teacher's,' she says. 'I am too old to climb. You are not.'

choices.text: Learn every page

effects.log: You learn the leaves by smell before you learn the characters. By the end of the year half the village comes to your door before they go to hers. She approves of this loudly.

choices.text: Keep climbing for her, every week

effects.log: Every week, a basket. She sorts it, you listen. When the knee finally lets her climb again, you climb together, slowly, and it is the best part of the week.

choices.text: Ask about the teacher who wrote it

effects.log: A young doctor who walked every road in the south and came back with a book and no money. 'Happiest person I ever knew.' You look at the book differently after that.

events.text: The young monk who rings the hill temple's dawn bell keeps oversleeping. You are always awake before the roosters anyway. One morning, in the grey, you climb the steps and look at the great log that swings against the bell.

choices.text: Ring it, exactly once, very hard

effects.log: BONG. Every dog in the valley howls. Every rooster gives up. The monk comes running out with his robe on backwards. You are not punished, quite.

choices.text: Wake the monk instead

effects.log: You shake him. He sits up, sees the light, gasps, and runs. The bell is rung only a little late. He brings you a steamed bun after, and a deal: wake him every morning.

choices.text: Ask the old abbot if you can learn to ring it

effects.log: The abbot considers you. 'There are a hundred and eight strokes. Each one is a breath. Can you count your breath?' You say yes. You cannot.

events.text: Every morning, a hundred and eight strokes. Slow ones first, then faster, then slow again. Today you lose count at sixty-three, and do not know whether to go on.

choices.text: Start the count again in your head and keep the rhythm

effects.log: The bell does not know you lost count. The valley does not know. Only you and the abbot, who says nothing, and gives you an extra bun.

choices.text: Stop and say you made a mistake

effects.log: The abbot nods. 'Then ring the rest well.' You ring forty-five more, each one careful. You think it is the best you have ever rung.

choices.text: Ring until it feels finished, without counting

effects.log: Somewhere near a hundred you stop thinking and only breathe. When you stop, it was a hundred and eight exactly. You do not know how.

events.text: The abbot is ill and the temple is full of worried monks. Someone has to ring the bell for the abbot's birthday, all hundred and eight, with the whole valley listening. They ask you.

choices.text: Ring it as the abbot taught you

effects.log: Slow, fast, slow. Your breath and the bell. Down in the valley people stop in the fields. In the abbot's room, the monks say, the old man smiled at stroke one hundred and eight.

choices.text: Ring it with the oversleeping monk, taking turns

effects.log: Fifty-four each. He does not oversleep. Both of you count aloud, and the valley hears two voices and one bell.

choices.text: Ask to ring it beside the abbot's window

effects.log: They carry the abbot's bed to the window. You ring, and the abbot counts under his breath, and gets it wrong at sixty-three, and laughs.

events.text: A troupe of shadow puppeteers sets up a lamp and a paper screen on the threshing floor. Behind the screen, as you creep around to look, a girl not much older than you is working three leather puppets at once.

choices.text: Ask how it is done

effects.log: She shows you: thin rods, the leather oiled so the light comes through red and gold. You manage to make a monkey fall over. It is the funniest thing anyone has ever seen.

choices.text: Help carry the lamp oil

effects.log: The troupe master pays you in a seat right at the front. You watch the Monkey King fight the whole of heaven, and come home with smoke in your eyes and stars in them too.

choices.text: Hold a puppet during the show

effects.log: You hold the dragon's tail. At the big moment you wave it so hard it tears. The crowd thinks it is part of the show. The troupe master gives you a long look.

events.text: The troupe is back. Their drummer has a fever. The troupe master looks at you, then at the drum, and raises an eyebrow very high.

choices.text: Drum for the Monkey King

ok.log: You drum the monkey's footsteps, the gods' anger and the thunder at the end. You only lose the beat once. The troupe master gives you a leather monkey with a broken rod.

fail.log: You drum the thunder too early and the whole of heaven loses its battle a scene before it should. The audience is delighted. The troupe is not.

choices.text: Say no, and nurse the drummer instead

effects.log: You bring broth and wet cloths. The drummer, who is about eleven, is very grateful and very embarrassed. They play the show without a drum, and it is quieter, and fine.

choices.text: Make the drum sounds with your mouth behind the screen

effects.log: It is ridiculous. It works. The crowd cannot tell where the booms come from, and the troupe master laughs so hard the lamp shakes.

events.text: Years later the troupe comes through once more, the girl with the three puppets now the troupe master. She remembers you. She has a new screen and an old monkey, and asks if you want to do the show with them tonight.

choices.text: Do the show

effects.log: Behind the screen, rod in hand, the village is only a shadow and a laugh. For two hours you are the Monkey King. When the lamp goes out, you are just yourself again, and a little bigger.

choices.text: Bring out the broken monkey they gave you

effects.log: She mends its rod with silk thread while you watch. 'There. Now it is yours properly.' The monkey dances on the screen that night, both of you working it.

choices.text: Sit in the front row and watch

effects.log: You sit where you sat at six. The show is better than you remember. The village children around you are open-mouthed. You were too, once. You still are.

events.text: Your first tooth comes out in a pear. You throw it on the roof for luck, the way you are supposed to. A magpie watches from the ridge, hops over, picks it up, and flies off with your tooth.

choices.text: Chase it, shouting

effects.log: You chase it across three roofs' worth of ground. It sits on the temple gate and looks down at you, unrepentant, with your tooth in its beak.

choices.text: Bow to it. Maybe that is the luck

effects.log: The magpie bows back. You are nearly sure it does. You tell everyone, and nobody believes you, which makes it better.

choices.text: Leave a grain of millet on the roof as a fair price

effects.log: The next morning the millet is gone. On the windowsill, in its place, is a shiny button.

events.text: The magpie keeps coming. It brings things to your windowsill: a button, a bead, a copper coin with a square hole, a blue thread. Today it brings a ring. Jade, carved with a tiger. It belongs to someone rich.

choices.text: Take it to the magistrate's house

effects.log: The magistrate's steward recognises it at once: it fell from the magistrate's sleeve in the garden in the spring. The steward pays you a silver bit and stares at the magpie on the gate.

choices.text: Hide it under your pillow

effects.log: It is beautiful. For three nights you are a rich child. On the fourth you cannot sleep for worry, and on the fifth you return it after all.

choices.text: Put it back on the sill for the magpie

effects.log: The magpie takes it back, offended, and you never see the ring again. You think somewhere there is a magpie nest with a jade tiger in it, which is better than a magistrate's sleeve.

events.text: The magpie is old now. It still comes. This morning, on the sill, there is a very small, very old, very white thing. It is a tooth. Yours. It kept it all these years.

choices.text: Keep the tooth in a little pouch

effects.log: You wear it on a cord. A tooth on a cord is a strange thing to wear. People ask. You tell them a magpie owed you, and paid.

choices.text: Throw it on the roof again, properly this time

effects.log: This time the magpie does not take it. It sits next to it on the ridge, like a guard. Luck, you decide, takes a while sometimes.

choices.text: Leave the magpie the best millet you can find

effects.log: A whole handful. The magpie eats like an emperor and then sits on the sill for an hour, close, closer than ever before, while you talk.

events.text: {npc} works the ferry across the river with a long pole and never says more than three words at once. When you sit on the landing stage every morning to watch, {npc} finally says: 'Want. To learn?'

choices.text: Say yes

mem.note: sat on my landing every morning

effects.log: {npc} hands you the pole. You fall in. {npc} fishes you out with the pole, which is apparently lesson one.

choices.text: Ask how {he} knows where the deep water is

effects.log: {npc} points at the water. 'Look.' You look. You see water. {npc} sighs. 'Look. Longer.' You look until lunch, and at the end you can see it: the dark seams where the river runs fast.

choices.text: Bring {npc} a bun instead

effects.log: {npc} eats it. Then nods at the seat in the boat. You ride across and back all morning, for free, in silence, perfectly happy.

events.text: In the ninth month {npc} takes you out on the river in the early cold and points at a thin skin of ice near the bank. 'Grey. Holds a cat. White. Holds a dog. Black. Holds nothing.' {He} makes you say it back, three times.

choices.text: Say it back until you dream it

effects.log: Grey holds a cat. White holds a dog. Black holds nothing. You will remember it your whole life, and you do not know yet how much that is worth.

choices.text: Ask what happened to make {him} so careful

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a long time. 'Brother. Black ice.' That is all. You do not ask again, and you listen to everything after that.

choices.text: Test the white ice with a stick

effects.log: It cracks under the stick with a sound like a whip. {npc} nods, once. 'Good. Now you know. Do not forget the sound.'

events.text: {npc}'s hands have gone stiff. In the spring floods the pole slips, and the ferry swings broadside in the fast water with a farmer, two goats and a basket of eggs aboard. {npc} looks at you.

choices.text: Take the pole and find the seam

mem.note: took the pole in the flood

ok.log: You find the dark seam and push. The ferry turns like an obedient ox. Goats, farmer and eggs reach the far bank. {npc} says four words: 'Good. Ferry is yours.'

fail.log: The pole skids, but you get the bow round enough to beach on a gravel bar. Two eggs break. The goats are fine. {npc} pats your shoulder twice, which from {him} is a speech.

choices.text: Steady {npc} and steer with {him}, four hands on the pole

mem.note: steered with me in the flood

effects.log: The two of you lean together into the current. The boat comes round slowly, the way the old ferry always did. You do not need words. You never did.

choices.text: Throw the rope to the bank and shout for help

effects.log: Three farmers haul you in. Nobody is hurt. That evening {npc} teaches you a knot you did not know, and says: 'Good. Rope is also a pole.'

events.text: {npc} from the lane has a spinning top painted with a red dragon, and has beaten every top in the village. {He} spins it on the flat stone outside the temple and looks at you. 'Yours is a turnip.'

choices.text: Spin your plain top against it

mem.note: knocked my dragon top off the stone

ok.log: Your plain top knocks the dragon off the stone. {npc} stares. 'Again.' You lose the next five. It does not matter. You beat the dragon once.

fail.log: The dragon top knocks yours into a puddle. {npc} laughs. You fish it out and decide, then and there, that this is war.

choices.text: Say a turnip is better than a dragon, because you can eat it

effects.log: {npc} has no answer to this. {He} is silent for an entire minute, which has never happened before.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how {he} spins it so long

effects.log: {npc} is so surprised to be asked that {he} shows you: wind the string tight, throw low. Rivals, it turns out, also like being asked.

events.text: You have whittled your own top from a jujube root, heavy and hard, and practised every evening. The lane gathers. {npc}'s dragon against your root, best of three, on the temple stone.

choices.text: Throw low and hard

mem.note: beat my dragon with a jujube root

ok.log: Two out of three. Your jujube top spins on alone while the dragon wobbles off the stone. The lane shrieks. {npc} goes red, then, slowly, grins.

fail.log: One out of three. Close. {npc} wins, and does not crow about it this time. {He} looks at your root top. 'Where did you get that wood?'

choices.text: Offer to trade tops for one round

effects.log: With the dragon you lose. With the root, {npc} wins. You both stare at each other. It was never the top. You both laugh for the first time.

choices.text: Let the small children play first

mem.note: let the little ones go first

effects.log: The little ones spin their turnips. {npc} grumbles, then shows one of them how to wind the string. Somehow the match never happens.

events.text: {npc} is leaving the village to be apprenticed in the town. On the last morning {he} comes to your door holding the red dragon top, the paint chipped, the string new.

choices.text: Give {npc} your jujube top in exchange

effects.log: You trade. Neither of you says anything soppy. Years later, you hear, {npc} still has a jujube top on {his} shelf in the town and will not let anyone touch it.

choices.text: Have one last match on the temple stone

effects.log: Best of three. Three draws, both tops spinning off together each time. You call it there. It is the right result.

choices.text: Tell {npc} {he} was the best in the village

effects.log: 'I know,' says {npc}. Then, quieter: 'You were second.' That is the nicest thing {npc} has ever said to anyone. You both know it.

events.text: You are chasing a hen through the market and crash into the calligrapher's table. A pot of ink goes over a whole scroll of the Thousand Character Classic, a commission, three weeks of work.

choices.text: Stay and say sorry

effects.log: The calligrapher, a thin man with ink to the elbows, looks at the scroll, at you, at the hen. 'You can grind ink for me until it is paid for.' It will take all summer.

choices.text: Run, then come back

effects.log: You run as far as the bridge, and stop, and walk back very slowly. The calligrapher is still standing over the ruined scroll. 'You came back,' he says. 'Good. Sit. Grind.'

choices.text: Blame the hen

effects.log: The hen does not deny it. The calligrapher almost smiles. 'Then the hen can grind ink. You will hold it.' You grind ink all summer anyway.

events.text: The debt was paid long ago, but you still come to grind ink: water, stone, the stick in slow circles, never fast, never pressing. The calligrapher watches the ink and not you. Today he says, 'Smell it.' It smells of pine smoke and rain.

choices.text: Ask to write one character with it

effects.log: He hands you a brush. You write 'eternal', the first character every student learns, eight strokes. He looks at it. 'Your hand is too fast. Your ink is good. Again.'

choices.text: Keep grinding until he says stop

effects.log: He does not say stop. You grind until the sun goes down, slow circles, and something in your shoulders loosens that you did not know was tight.

choices.text: Ask why the circles must be slow

effects.log: 'Fast ink is grey ink. Fast hand is grey hand.' He shows you a scroll by an old master whose characters look slow even though you know they were brushed in a breath.

events.text: The commission is due again: the Thousand Character Classic, for the same patron. The calligrapher's hand has begun to shake. He gives you the brush. 'The first line. Then I will do the rest.'

choices.text: Write the first line slowly

effects.log: Heaven earth dark yellow, the universe vast and boundless. Your characters are not as good as his. They are not bad. The patron never notices which line is which.

choices.text: Write it fast and bold, in your own way

effects.log: It is wrong for the scroll and the calligrapher winces. Then he looks again, and keeps it. 'That one is yours. It will be good one day.'

choices.text: Grind his ink, and steady the paper while he writes

effects.log: His hand shakes less with someone holding the paper. He writes all thousand characters. On the last one, he lets you hold the brush with him.

events.text: The village smith needs someone to pump the bellows. The pay is a bowl of noodles a day and the heat is like standing in the sun's mouth. You take it.

choices.text: Pump steady, all day

effects.log: Push, pull, push, pull. The coals breathe white. By evening your arms are jelly and the smith says, without looking: 'Good fire.' You will remember those two words a long time.

choices.text: Watch the iron instead of the fire

effects.log: You see how the colour tells the heat: dull red, cherry, orange, butter-yellow. The smith catches you staring and quizzes you. You get them all right.

choices.text: Ask to hit something

effects.log: The smith gives you a tiny hammer and a nail to straighten. It takes you an hour. The nail is less straight at the end. The smith laughs, a big laugh, like the bellows.

events.text: Between jobs the smith lets you forge your own nail, start to finish. You decide, privately, that it will be a sword. A very small one.

choices.text: Heat it to butter-yellow and draw it out

ok.log: It comes out as long as your hand, crooked, with an edge on one side. A sword. Sort of. The smith files a point on it and calls it a 'nail of distinction'.

fail.log: You overheat it and it sparkles like a firework and crumbles. The smith says every smith burns one. Then he gives you another nail.

choices.text: Make an actual nail, a perfect one

effects.log: It is the best nail you can make. The smith puts it in the beam over the door with a single blow. 'There. Holding the house up.' It is.

choices.text: Make a hook for the kitchen at home

effects.log: It is lopsided. It holds the ladle. It is used every day for years.

events.text: The smith has a bundle wrapped in sacking for you. Inside is a practice sword, blunt, balanced, its iron grey and plain. 'For the bellows,' the smith says. 'Five summers of bellows.'

choices.text: Swing it in the yard until dark

effects.log: It is heavier than a stick and lighter than you feared. By dark your arm knows its weight. By the end of the year, so does the rest of you.

choices.text: Ask the smith to teach you to keep it

effects.log: Oil, cloth, never leave it wet, never let it rust. The smith says a sword that is looked after looks after you. You believe it.

choices.text: Show the smith your old nail sword beside it

effects.log: The smith picks up the crooked little nail sword, turns it over, and for a moment looks very young. 'I made one of these too.' It goes on the shelf by the forge.

events.text: On the morning of the Mid-Autumn Festival, three mooncakes have vanished from the cooling rack in the yard. There are crumbs on the wall. There are tiny footprints in the flour. Everyone suspects your cousin.

choices.text: Examine the footprints

effects.log: Four toes, small, in a line. Not a cousin. Not a cat. You follow them along the wall to a hole under the woodshed.

choices.text: Defend your cousin

effects.log: Nobody believes either of you. You both sulk on the step. It is the closest you and your cousin have ever been.

choices.text: Set a trap with the last mooncake

effects.log: You tie a thread to it and wait up behind the water jar. You fall asleep. In the morning the thread is chewed through and the mooncake is gone.

events.text: Mid-Autumn again, and you are hiding behind the woodshed at dusk. You see the thief: a raccoon dog, fat and stripy-faced, with three cubs behind her, all of them eating a mooncake as if it was the moon itself.

choices.text: Watch them quietly

effects.log: The cubs tumble over each other for the crumbs. The mother looks at you and does not run. You decide never to tell anyone where the mooncakes went.

choices.text: Tell the grown-ups

effects.log: The grown-ups come with a lamp and a stick. By the time they get there, the woodshed is empty. Your cousin is cleared. You feel, oddly, that you have betrayed someone.

choices.text: Leave them a piece of your own mooncake

effects.log: The lotus paste one, your favourite. In the morning it is gone and there is a dead mouse on the step, which you decide is a thank you.

events.text: Mid-Autumn again. The moon is enormous. Behind the woodshed there are new cubs now, and the old raccoon dog, grey at the muzzle, sitting in the moonlight as if waiting for something.

choices.text: Bring a whole mooncake out to the woodshed

effects.log: You break it in five. The old one takes the last piece, slowly, from almost your hand. You sit with them under the moon until your family calls you in.

choices.text: Show your cousin, at last

effects.log: Your cousin stares, then laughs until crying. 'All these years. All those beatings.' You both sit and watch them eat. It is a good festival.

choices.text: Make a mooncake shaped like a raccoon dog

effects.log: It looks like a lumpy pig. The family is baffled. You put it on the woodshed wall, and in the morning it is gone, and there is no mouse, just tiny footprints in a row.

events.text: The county's calendar clerk, a tired official with ink on the nose, comes to the village every year to watch the sky from the hill. This year you follow. 'Can you count?' the clerk asks. 'Then count those.'

choices.text: Count the stars in the Dipper's bowl

effects.log: Four. Then you count the faint ones, and there are more, and more. The clerk laughs. 'Now you know why this job never ends.'

choices.text: Ask why the stars matter

effects.log: 'Because the emperor's calendar has to be right, or the farmers plant on the wrong day and the empire starves.' You look at the sky as if it were a field.

choices.text: Hold the lantern so the clerk can write

effects.log: All night, the lantern steady in your two hands. At dawn the clerk lets you look at the chart: hundreds of tiny dots, in the clerk's tiny hand, and one smudge, where you sneezed.

events.text: Clear winter night, alone on the hill. Near the Weaver Star there is a star that was not there last week. You are sure of it. Fairly sure. It has a faint smear, like a brush lifted too soon.

choices.text: Draw where it is, every night for a month

effects.log: Every night, one dot. The dots move. Slowly, in a line, like a cart on a road. You have no idea what it means, and it is the most exciting thing in the world.

choices.text: Tell the village it is an omen

effects.log: The village argues for a week whether it is a good omen or a bad one. Nobody plants anything differently. The star does not care.

choices.text: Make a wish on it

effects.log: You wish for something you will not tell anyone, ever. The smear-star goes on across the sky as if it is taking the wish somewhere.

events.text: The calendar clerk comes back, older, and goes white when you show the month of dots. 'A broom star. Nobody in the county office saw it. They were all indoors.' The clerk looks at you as if for the first time.

choices.text: Give the clerk your drawings for the record

effects.log: Your dots go into the county's star book, under the clerk's name and, in small characters, yours. Somewhere in the capital, a very old astronomer reads it.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to teach you the whole sky

effects.log: Every winter after that, the clerk comes, and you climb the hill together, and the sky stops being a ceiling and becomes a map.

choices.text: Keep the drawings, and keep watching

effects.log: Some things are worth more kept. You watch the sky every clear night for the rest of your childhood. It never gets dull.

events.text: Chasing a sparrow into the loft, you put your hand on something long, wrapped in oiled cloth, tied to a rafter where nobody would ever look. Under the dust the cloth is good silk. Under the silk is a sword.

choices.text: Unwrap it, just a little

effects.log: A hand's width of blade, grey and clean, with a nick near the hilt. It is not a farmer's thing. It is not a merchant's thing. You wrap it again exactly as it was, heart hammering.

choices.text: Leave it and say nothing

effects.log: You climb down very carefully. At dinner you look at your parents' hands, which have calluses in places you never noticed before.

choices.text: Run and ask your parents about it

effects.log: The table goes quiet. A long look passes between your parents. 'When you are older,' one says. It is the first time that sentence has ever sounded frightened.

events.text: A traveller with a scar through one eyebrow stops at the gate and asks your parents, very politely, whether they remember the Three Pines Inn. Your parent says no. Your parent's hand, you notice, is shaking.

choices.text: Bring the traveller tea and watch

effects.log: The traveller drinks it, looks at your parent for a long time, and finally laughs. 'No. I suppose you do not.' The traveller leaves a copper on the table for the tea and goes.

choices.text: Stand in the doorway beside your parent

effects.log: You are small and the doorway is big. But the traveller sees you, and something in the scarred face softens. 'Yours?' A nod. 'Then you chose well.' And goes.

choices.text: Slip up to the loft and check the sword is there

effects.log: It is. When you come down, the traveller is gone, and your parent is sitting on the step with both hands over the face, and you sit too, and say nothing.

events.text: One evening your parent climbs to the loft and comes down with the sword. 'You found this years ago,' your parent says. 'I know. You put the knot back wrong.' And then, for the first time, the story: a young wanderer, a bad year, a choice to stop.

choices.text: Ask to be taught one move

effects.log: In the yard, under the moon, your parent teaches you one move: draw, cut, return the blade. Your parent's body still knows it perfectly, and for a moment looks twenty years younger.

choices.text: Ask why they stopped

effects.log: 'Because I wanted a door I could close at night.' Your parent looks at the house, at you. 'It was the bravest thing I ever did.' You think about that for years.

choices.text: Ask to keep the secret, always

effects.log: Your parent laughs, ruffles your hair, and puts the sword back in the rafters, with you holding the ladder. The knot is right this time.

events.text: Market day in the county town. Your parent gives you three copper coins and says: 'Buy something. But first, look at everything.' It is the most coins you have ever held.

choices.text: Look at everything, as told

effects.log: Sugar figures, a man swallowing a sword, a cage of crickets, an old woman selling needles. By the time you have looked at everything the coins are warm and you have bought nothing.

choices.text: Buy a sugar figure at once

effects.log: It is a phoenix and it is gone in four bites. You have two coins left and a sticky face. Your parent laughs and says nothing, which is a lesson in itself.

choices.text: Buy a needle for the old woman's sake

effects.log: She looks at you, three coppers, and gives you two needles and a sweet. Your parent, watching from the noodle stall, looks proud.

events.text: A peddler sells you a 'jade' frog for two coppers. On the way home it rains, and the jade frog turns into a green stain on your palm. It was painted soap.

choices.text: Go back next market and confront the peddler

effects.log: The peddler pretends not to know you. You hold up your green palm. The crowd laughs. The peddler gives your coppers back, very red, to make you go away.

choices.text: Learn how to tell real jade

effects.log: Your parent shows you: real jade is cold, heavy, and does not scratch with a copper. You test everything you see for a year. Mostly with your teeth.

choices.text: Keep the stain as a reminder

effects.log: It fades in a week. The lesson does not. Your parent says it was the best two coppers you ever spent.

events.text: This market day your parent is sick, and you go alone with the cart: two sacks of beans, a basket of eggs, and instructions not to come back with less than the eggs are worth.

choices.text: Haggle for every copper

ok.log: You sell the beans to the noodle shop at a fair price and the eggs to a cook who laughs at your bargaining and pays it anyway. You come home with more than your parent hoped.

fail.log: The bean merchant beats you down a little. You come home with enough, and a sore throat, and very many opinions about bean merchants.

choices.text: Test every coin with a copper before you take it

effects.log: One of them is lead dipped in copper. You hand it back without a word. The buyer looks at you, startled, and pays properly.

choices.text: Sell quickly and come home to your parent

effects.log: You sell at the first fair price and hurry home with medicine from the herb stall. Your parent says you did exactly right, and means it.

events.text: A fever comes in the deep of winter. You burn and shiver. You remember very little except a lamp that never goes out, a cool cloth, and someone's voice that keeps telling you the story of the cowherd and the weaver, over and over.

choices.text: Hold on to the voice

effects.log: On the fourth night the fever breaks. You open your eyes and your parent is asleep sitting up, the cloth still in hand, the story still half-said.

choices.text: Ask for the end of the story

effects.log: 'The magpies make a bridge,' your parent whispers, 'and they meet.' And you sleep, and in the morning the fever is gone.

choices.text: Count the lamp's flickers

effects.log: You count to a thousand, and then to a thousand again. Your parent never lets the lamp go out. You learn something about patience you will not understand until much later.

events.text: You are well. Your parent is not: the same fever, the same winter, years later. The house is very quiet. Somebody has to keep the lamp lit.

choices.text: Keep the lamp and the cloth, all night

effects.log: You stay awake the whole night, changing the cloth, feeding the lamp. Near dawn, without opening their eyes, your parent says: 'The magpies make a bridge.'

choices.text: Run through the snow for the doctor

effects.log: The doctor is old and grumpy and comes anyway, cursing the snow. You carry the lamp ahead the whole way. The medicine works by morning.

choices.text: Tell the story of the cowherd and the weaver

effects.log: Over and over, the way it was told to you. Sometimes you fall asleep in the middle. When you wake, you start again.

events.text: Spring. Your parent is on the step in the sun, thin, laughing at the chickens. They pull you down to sit. 'Do you know,' they say, 'you told it wrong. You had the ox fly.'

choices.text: Insist the ox flies

effects.log: 'The ox definitely flies.' You argue about it for an hour. It is the best argument you have ever had.

choices.text: Ask them to tell it properly, one more time

effects.log: They tell it slowly, in the sun. You are too old for it now. You listen anyway, to every word.

choices.text: Say nothing, and lean against them

effects.log: Your parent's arm goes round you. The chickens squabble. The sun is warm. Nothing else is needed.

events.text: You knock the blue-and-white bowl off the shelf. It was your great-grandmother's, the only fine thing in the house. It is in four pieces on the floor and nobody is home yet.

choices.text: Confess the moment they come in

effects.log: Your parent looks at the pieces for a long time. Then at you. 'You told me,' your parent says. 'That matters more than a bowl.' It still matters a lot. You can tell.

choices.text: Hide the pieces under the bed

effects.log: For three days you cannot look at anyone. On the fourth day your parent finds the pieces while sweeping, and says nothing at all, which is worse than anything.

choices.text: Try to glue it with rice paste

effects.log: The bowl holds together until someone looks at it. Your parent, coming in, sees the rice paste and laughs before they can stop themself, and then you are both laughing.

events.text: A bowl-mender comes through the village with a little drill worked by a bow-string and a box of copper staples. He can rivet broken porcelain so it holds water again. It costs money. More than you have.

choices.text: Offer to work for him for a day

effects.log: You fetch water, hold bowls, turn the bow-drill. At sunset he mends your bowl with nine copper staples, neat as stitches. It holds water. It looks like a map of rivers.

choices.text: Watch him all day and learn how

effects.log: Drill, staple, wax, never press. By evening you know how it is done. You do not have the drill. You have the knowing.

choices.text: Give him your copper coins and the eggs you collected

effects.log: He counts it, shakes his head, and mends it anyway, for the eggs. 'Old bowls deserve it,' he says. 'And honest children.'

events.text: At a family gathering an aunt picks up the mended bowl with its nine copper staples and makes a face. 'Why do you keep this broken thing?'

choices.text: Tell the story of how it broke

effects.log: You tell all of it: the shelf, the four pieces, the bowl-mender. The aunt puts it down very gently. Your parent, across the room, is smiling into the tea.

choices.text: Say: it is stronger now

effects.log: The staples are copper; the bowl was only clay. It is true. The aunt, to her own surprise, agrees. You are given the bowl to keep, when you are grown.

choices.text: Fill it with tea and drink from it

effects.log: It holds. Of course it holds. The aunt watches you drink from the mended bowl and says, quietly, that her mother had one like it.

events.text: At night, through the wall, you hear your parents counting coins and going quiet. The rent is due. There is not enough. In the morning nobody says anything, and breakfast is thinner.

choices.text: Start collecting eggs from the hens to sell

effects.log: You get up before the roosters and find every hidden nest. By the end of the month you have a little bag of coppers under a floorboard.

choices.text: Catch fish in the stream to sell

effects.log: You catch seven small fish in a week and sell them to the inn for a copper each. The cook says if you can catch more, the inn will buy them.

choices.text: Pretend you heard nothing

effects.log: You eat less without being asked and say you are not hungry. Your parents notice. Parents always notice.

events.text: The landlord's steward comes to the gate. Your parents are being polite in the way that means they are frightened. The steward is looking around the yard for something worth taking.

choices.text: Bring out your bag of coppers

effects.log: Everyone stares at the bag in your hands. It is not enough for the whole rent. It is enough for the steward to go away until next month. Your parent cannot speak.

choices.text: Offer the steward a cup of water, very politely

effects.log: The steward, thrown by a polite child, drinks it, and is slightly less unpleasant, and gives your family another month.

choices.text: Stand by your parents and say nothing

effects.log: The steward looks at your face and goes. Later your parent says: 'I saw you. You stood like a little wall.'

events.text: The harvest is good this year. The rent is paid. Your parent finds the little loose floorboard where your bag used to be, and puts something under it before telling you to look.

choices.text: Look under the floorboard

effects.log: Three coppers, and a wooden hen, carved badly, with your name scratched on the bottom. 'For the best egg-finder in the county.' You keep it for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Say they should not have

effects.log: 'You put the coppers there first,' your parent says. 'I am only paying back with interest.' And laughs, the old laugh from before the bad year.

choices.text: Ask to keep earning, now that you know how

effects.log: Your parents look at each other. Then they give you the hens properly, your own to keep. The money is small. Being trusted with it is not.

events.text: The old neighbour's persimmon tree hangs over the wall, heavy and orange. The neighbour is deaf, grumpy and rumoured to have been a soldier. Every child in the lane has dared every other to climb it.

choices.text: Climb it at dusk

effects.log: You get three persimmons and a torn trouser. As you drop over the wall, the old neighbour is standing right there, arms folded, having watched the whole thing.

choices.text: Knock on the gate and ask for one

effects.log: The neighbour stares at you, deaf, and you have to shout. 'A persimmon? You ASKED?' You get four. Nobody has asked in thirty years.

choices.text: Pick up the windfalls in the lane only

effects.log: The fallen ones, bruised and sweet. The neighbour, watching from the window, thinks you are an unusually honest child. You are just afraid of the tree.

events.text: The old neighbour beckons you through the gate. On a bamboo frame, hundreds of peeled persimmons hang drying in the sun like little lanterns. 'Help,' the neighbour shouts. 'Or no persimmons. Ever.'

choices.text: Peel, string and hang them all afternoon

effects.log: Your hands are orange for a week. The neighbour tells you war stories at a shout, very badly, while you work. You love every one.

choices.text: Bring the other children to help

effects.log: Five children, one grumpy soldier and a thousand persimmons. By sunset the lane smells of sugar and the neighbour is pretending not to smile.

choices.text: Ask why so many, for one person

effects.log: The neighbour looks at the frames. 'For the ones who did not come home,' the old voice says, much quieter. 'Every year. One string each.' You count them. There are many.

events.text: Winter. The dried persimmons are ready, frosted white with their own sugar. The old neighbour is too stiff to carry them to the shrine on the hill this year.

choices.text: Carry them up the hill for the neighbour

effects.log: One string for each name, hung at the shrine. You do not know the names. You hang them carefully anyway. The neighbour watches from the bottom of the hill, very straight.

choices.text: Take the neighbour up, slowly, on your arm

effects.log: It takes the whole morning. At the top the neighbour says each name aloud, and you hang each string, and nobody is in a hurry.

choices.text: Eat one, as the neighbour orders

effects.log: 'They wanted them eaten,' the neighbour shouts. 'Not looked at.' It is the sweetest thing you have ever tasted, and a little sad.

events.text: In spring a pair of swallows builds a mud nest under the eaves over the door. Everyone says swallows bring luck to a house. Everyone also has to step over the droppings.

choices.text: Put a board under the nest for the mess

effects.log: It works. The swallows ignore you. The family praises your cleverness. You watch the nest every morning, waiting.

choices.text: Count the trips they make with mud

effects.log: Two hundred and eleven by evening, and you lose count when you sneeze. A nest is a lot of work. You respect them.

choices.text: Leave out water in a dish for them

effects.log: They do not drink from the dish. A sparrow does. You decide the sparrow can stay too.

events.text: Four chicks, open-beaked, shrieking. One falls out of the nest onto the step, bald and furious.

choices.text: Climb up and put it back

effects.log: You do it on a stool on a stool, very carefully. The parents dive at your head the whole time. The chick goes back in. It shrieks louder than the others. It is yours now.

choices.text: Keep it in a basket and feed it flies

effects.log: It eats seventy flies. You are exhausted. The swallow parents come and feed it on the step, and you realise they never stopped.

choices.text: Call your family to help

effects.log: Your family rigs a little ladder and up it goes. Everyone stands under the eaves watching the nest for an hour instead of working.

events.text: This spring the swallows do not come back. The empty mud nest sits under the eaves. Nobody says anything about luck. And then, three weeks late, a swallow flies straight at the door and into the nest as if it had never left.

choices.text: Shout for everyone to come and see

effects.log: The whole house comes out. Even the grumpiest uncle smiles. It is one swallow, then two. Late, but home.

choices.text: Wonder if it is the chick you put back

effects.log: It is impossible to know. It has a little white mark near the beak, the way the fallen one did. You decide it is.

choices.text: Think about what late means

effects.log: Not never. Only late. You think about that for a long time, sitting on the step, while the swallows mend the old nest above you.

events.text: You fold a paper boat, write the only characters you know on it, 'hello' and 'who', and put it on the stream that runs down out of the village toward the river. It spins once and is gone.

choices.text: Send another every day

effects.log: A whole fleet sails out of the village that month. The stream is very busy. You do not expect anything back. That is the point of boats.

choices.text: Draw a picture on it of where you live

effects.log: A house, a stream, a big tree, a very bad dog. You put your whole world on a paper boat and let it go.

choices.text: Put a dried plum inside as a gift

effects.log: Whoever finds it, you think, will at least get a plum. It is the kindest thought you have had all week.

events.text: A paper boat comes UP the stream. That is not possible. It has been carried by somebody, wet and careful, and left on the stepping stone where you launch yours. On it, in a child's crooked hand: 'me. who are you.'

choices.text: Write back your name

effects.log: You write it as well as you can, and add 'by the big tree'. You wait a week. Then two. A boat comes back: a name, and 'by the mill'. The mill village is a day downstream.

choices.text: Send a whole poem

effects.log: It is four lines about the dog. The reply is four lines about a goat. A correspondence is born.

choices.text: Go down the stream to look for them

effects.log: You walk until the stream meets the river and you are frightened by how big the world is. You go home. But now you know the way.

events.text: Years of boats. The letters are longer now and come by the fish-seller instead of the stream. {npc}, the child by the mill, writes: the mill fair is in ten days. Come.

choices.text: Walk the day downstream to the fair

mem.note: came all the way to the mill fair

effects.log: You know each other at once, somehow, by the way you both stand looking at the stream. {npc} has brought every boat you ever sent, in a box, dried flat.

choices.text: Send a boat to say you cannot come, and why

effects.log: {npc} writes back so fast the fish-seller complains. 'Then I come to you.' And does, at the next festival, with a goat.

choices.text: Make the biggest boat yet and sail it to the fair

effects.log: It sinks at the first bend. You walk the rest of the way, laughing, and arrive soaked. {npc} laughs so hard the goat runs away.

events.text: {npc}, who lives two doors down and is your best ally in all things, is sick in bed with a cough that will not go. The healer says rest, a whole month. {npc} has never been still for a month in {his} life.

choices.text: Visit every day with news of the lane

mem.note: came every day when I was sick

effects.log: You tell {npc} everything: who fell in the pond, what the dog stole. {npc} laughs, and coughs, and makes you tell it again.

choices.text: Bring a cricket in a pot to keep {him} company

effects.log: The cricket sings all night. {npc}'s parents are less pleased than {npc} is.

choices.text: Copy out the storyteller's tale for {npc} to read

effects.log: Your characters are terrible. {npc} reads it anyway, three times, and corrects your spelling in the margin.

events.text: The cough has come back with the summer, and {npc} is in bed again, staring at the dark window. 'I miss the fireflies,' {he} says. The paddies outside are full of them, drifting like slow green sparks.

choices.text: Catch a jar of them

ok.log: You come back with a jar full of little green lights, glowing and fading. {npc} holds it in both hands and does not cough for an hour.

mem.note: fell in the paddy for my fireflies

fail.log: You fall in the paddy twice and catch six. Six is enough. {npc} names every one of them.

choices.text: Prop {npc} up at the window to watch

effects.log: You open the shutter and help {him} up on the pillows. The two of you watch the paddies glow until {npc} falls asleep against the frame.

choices.text: Hold up a paper lantern and dance around the yard like one

mem.note: danced like a firefly for me

effects.log: You are a very large, very silly firefly. {npc} laughs until the healer comes and shouts at you both.

events.text: {npc} is well. The first thing {he} does, out of bed, is drag you to the paddies at dusk, carrying the jar, to set the fireflies free where they came from.

choices.text: Open the jar together

mem.note: let the fireflies go with me

effects.log: They drift out one by one, slow, and then all together, and are lost among the others. {npc} says: 'Thank you.' It is the only time either of you ever says it out loud.

choices.text: Race {npc} back to the village

mem.note: raced me home from the paddies

effects.log: {npc} wins, of course, after a month in bed, out of sheer spite. You are both very glad.
