choices.text: Promise to always be there when {npc} is sick

mem.note: promised to be there when I am sick

effects.log: {npc} snorts. 'And I for you.' It is a children's promise. It turns out to be one of the ones that is kept.

events.text: In the mud after the rain you find a coin. Not a copper: something older, greenish, with a square hole and four characters you cannot read. It is very heavy for something so small.

choices.text: Thread it on a string around your neck

effects.log: It bumps against your chest when you run. You decide it is lucky. Proving this will take years.

choices.text: Show it to the village teacher

effects.log: The teacher squints, then goes very still. 'This is from the dynasty before the dynasty before. Keep it safe.' You have never felt so important.

choices.text: Spend it at the sweet stall

effects.log: The sweet seller looks at it, laughs, and gives it back with a free sweet. 'I would not know how to give change for that.'

events.text: A collector passing through the village hears about your coin. He offers you a whole silver tael for it, which is more money than you have ever imagined.

choices.text: Sell it

effects.log: A whole tael. You buy your family a new pot, yourself a knife, and still have most of it left. The coin goes away in the collector's purse. Sometimes you miss its weight.

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: The collector shakes his head at foolish children and goes. You are not sure it was the right choice. It feels like the right choice.

choices.text: Ask him what the characters say

effects.log: He reads them for you: 'Peace and plenty for ten thousand years.' He does not offer to buy it again. 'A coin like that, better worn than sold,' he says.

events.text: You slip on the muddy bank above the fast water. Your hand shoots out and closes on a root, and the coin on its string swings out over the river and back, and taps you on the chin, as if to say: careful.

choices.text: Decide the coin really is lucky

effects.log: You climb back up, shaking. The string is fine. The coin is fine. From that day you never take it off.

choices.text: Decide the root is lucky

effects.log: You go back the next day and thank the root. A bank of roots, you decide, is better than any coin. You are probably right.

choices.text: Learn to swim, properly

effects.log: The fisherman's children teach you. It is cold and humiliating and by the end of the summer you can cross the river. Luck, you think, needs help.

events.arc: The Little Drummer of the Dragon Boat
events.text: The Dragon Boat Festival. The village's junior boat has twelve paddlers and no drummer, because the drummer has the mumps. The captain, a big child of fourteen, looks along the riverbank and points at you.

choices.text: Say yes at once

effects.log: You sit in the dragon's head with a drum between your knees. You have no idea what you are doing. You hit the drum. Twelve paddles hit the water. You suddenly have an idea.

choices.text: Say you cannot keep time

effects.log: 'Can you count to two?' says the captain. 'Then you can drum.' You can count to two. You drum.

choices.text: Suggest someone else

effects.log: Nobody else wants to. The captain picks you anyway. You practise on an upturned bucket all week until the neighbours beg you to stop.

events.arc: The Little Drummer of the Dragon Boat
events.text: Race day. Three junior boats on the river. Yours is last off the line. The paddlers are splashing out of time, panicking. They are all looking at you and the drum.

choices.text: Drum slower, not faster

ok.log: Slow. Deep. Together. The paddles find it, all twelve, and the boat leaps. You pass one boat and catch the other on the line. A draw. The village goes mad.

fail.log: You drum slower and they slow down too. You come third. The captain says it was the right idea and the wrong day.

choices.text: Drum as hard and fast as you can

effects.log: Fast, fast, fast. The paddlers go mad, the boat zigzags, and somehow you come second. Your hands hurt for days.

choices.text: Shout the rhythm instead of drumming

effects.log: 'One, TWO! One, TWO!' Your voice carries across the whole river. Other boats' paddlers start following your count. Chaos. Glorious chaos.

events.arc: The Little Drummer of the Dragon Boat
events.text: You are too big for the drum now. You are a paddler. In the dragon's head sits a small, terrified child, holding the sticks as if they were snakes.

choices.text: Tell the child your secret: slower, not faster

effects.log: The child nods, white-faced. On the day, the child drums slow and deep, and the boat finds it, and you, at the third paddle, grin into the spray.

choices.text: Paddle so hard the child does not have to be perfect

effects.log: You pull until your shoulders burn. The boat goes. Nobody hears the drum mistakes over the cheering.

choices.text: Let the child set any rhythm, and follow it

effects.log: It is a strange, hopping rhythm. The whole crew learns it. The village calls it the frog beat. It wins the race. It is still drummed every year.

events.text: A swordsman in a dusty blue robe ties a tall grey horse at the village well and goes into the inn. The horse is thirsty, and the well bucket is out of its reach.

choices.text: Draw water for the horse

effects.log: It drinks four buckets. It puts its great soft nose against your cheek. When the swordsman comes out, the horse refuses to leave until you have scratched its ears.

choices.text: Watch the sword instead of the horse

effects.log: When the swordsman comes out you are staring at the sword so hard that the stranger laughs. 'It is just iron, little one. The horse is the valuable one.'

choices.text: Ask the horse's name

effects.log: 'Cloud,' says the swordsman, surprised. 'Nobody asks the horse's name.' Cloud is given a handful of beans from your pocket.

events.text: Two years later, a tall grey horse comes alone down the road and stops at the well, saddled, riderless, with a cut on its shoulder. It looks at you as if it remembers.

choices.text: Care for its cut and keep it safe

effects.log: You wash the cut with salt water the way the herb woman taught. The horse lets you. For a week it lives in the headman's barn, and you visit every day.

choices.text: Follow its tracks back up the road

effects.log: You follow them until the light goes. Nothing. You come home late, scolded, and the horse is waiting at your gate.

choices.text: Call it by name

effects.log: 'Cloud.' Its ears come forward. It is the same horse. You are certain now. Then where is the swordsman?

events.text: The swordsman comes, limping, with one arm in a sling. Cloud whinnies across the whole village. The stranger looks at the horse, and at you, for a long time.

choices.text: Give Cloud back

effects.log: The swordsman bows to you, a real bow, the kind given to equals. 'Twice you have watered my horse. Remember my name. If ever you need a sword, send word.'

choices.text: Ask what happened

effects.log: 'An ambush on the pass. Cloud ran. Good horse.' The swordsman scratches the grey ears exactly where you used to. 'It ran to the one place it trusted.'

choices.text: Ask to be taught to ride

effects.log: The swordsman, laughing, puts you on Cloud's back and walks the two of you around the well three times. It is like riding a mountain. It is the best morning of your life.

events.text: The riverbank clay is perfect: grey, smooth, and it holds a shape. You decide to make an army. Generals, archers, a cavalry of very lumpy horses.

choices.text: Make a hundred tiny soldiers

effects.log: It takes the whole summer. They dry on the windowsill in ranks. Your family is not allowed to touch the windowsill.

choices.text: Make one big general, as tall as your knee

effects.log: He has a beard, a fierce face and one arm that keeps falling off. You name him General Fall-Off. He is your favourite thing in the world.

choices.text: Make an army of cats instead

effects.log: Cat archers. Cat cavalry, riding bigger cats. The village children come to see it and beg you to make them one.

events.text: The village potter sees your army on the windowsill and stops dead. 'You did not fire these.' You did not know clay could be fired. The potter's kiln is lit tomorrow.

choices.text: Let the potter fire them

effects.log: Half of them crack in the heat. The other half come out red and hard and ring like little bells when you tap them. They will last a thousand years, the potter says.

choices.text: Ask the potter to teach you the wheel

effects.log: The wheel throws your first bowl across the room. The second is a bowl, nearly. The potter nods. 'Come back.'

choices.text: Keep them as they are

effects.log: Unfired, they will crumble one day. You know that now. You keep them anyway, for exactly as long as they last.

events.text: Digging a new well, the villagers break into something old under the field: a little chamber, and in it, rows of clay soldiers, old as the hills, tiny, fired, ringing faintly when the spade touches them.

choices.text: Go down with a lamp and look

effects.log: Rows and rows. Somebody, long ago, made them for somebody they loved. You recognise a lumpy horse that looks just like one of yours, and you laugh, alone in the dark.

choices.text: Put one of your fired soldiers in with them

effects.log: One red soldier, among the grey ones. In a thousand years someone will dig here and be very confused. You like that.

choices.text: Help the villagers seal it back up, untouched

effects.log: The headman says it belongs to whoever made it. You agree. You help fill it back in, carefully, and plant a peach tree on top.

events.text: There are eleven orphans at the temple and one rice pot, and the rice is measured with a wooden scoop. The newest, a tiny child who arrived in a basket last month, always gets the burnt scrapings at the bottom.

choices.text: Swap bowls with the little one

effects.log: You eat the burnt part. It is bitter and crunchy. The little one eats your white rice and looks at you as if you were the Buddha himself.

choices.text: Sneak a scoop from the store at night

effects.log: The rice store is locked, but the lock is old. You get one scoop into the little one's bowl before dawn. In the morning the old abbot looks at the scoop, and at you, and says nothing.

choices.text: Tell the cook monk it is not fair

effects.log: The cook monk is surprised to be told anything by a child. He thinks about it, and then stirs the pot before serving, so the burnt part goes to everyone a little.

events.text: The old abbot calls you to the kitchen. On the table: the rice pot, the scoop, and the key to the rice store. 'Someone,' the abbot says mildly, 'has been feeding the little one. Someone should be in charge of the pot.'

choices.text: Accept, and measure fairly

effects.log: Every grain counted, every bowl the same, the burnt part shared. It is a terrible job. Everyone complains to you instead of to the abbot. You understand the abbot much better now.

choices.text: Confess about the scoop first

effects.log: 'I know,' says the abbot. 'That is why the key is yours. A thief who steals for another knows what the rice is for.'

choices.text: Say the cook monk should keep it

effects.log: The abbot nods. 'Then you will help him.' You end up with the key anyway. Abbots, you learn, always get their way.

events.text: A hard winter. The rice will not last until the spring alms. Eleven children, and twelve now, and the store half empty. The abbot is old and tired. Everyone is looking at the keeper of the pot.

choices.text: Make the rice into thin porridge to stretch it

effects.log: Thin porridge for two months. Nobody is full. Nobody starves. In the spring the abbot says it was the wisest thing done in that temple in years.

choices.text: Go down to the village and ask for alms yourself

effects.log: You walk from door to door in the snow with the begging bowl. People who never gave to the monks give to you. You come back with half a sack.

choices.text: Gather pine nuts and roots on the hill to add to the pot

effects.log: Your hands crack in the cold. But the pot is fuller. The little one, who is not so little now, comes with you every day.

events.text: At the temple orphanage, the other children are talking about birthdays. One knows the day. Two think they know. Nobody knows yours. It was never written down.

choices.text: Pick one yourself

effects.log: You pick the day of the first snow, because it is the best day. The other children argue that you cannot choose. You can, it turns out. Nobody can stop you.

choices.text: Pick the day you arrived at the temple

effects.log: The abbot looks in the register for you. Spring, the third month, the fifteenth day. It is not when you were born. It is when you were found. That is better.

choices.text: Decide birthdays do not matter

effects.log: You say so loudly. That night you lie awake thinking about it. Birthdays matter a bit.

events.text: On your chosen day, you expect nothing. At the evening meal, the cook monk puts a bowl in front of you with a boiled egg in it, dyed red. The other children are all trying very hard not to look at you.

choices.text: Eat it slowly, the whole thing

effects.log: It is just an egg. It is the best thing you have ever eaten. The little ones watch every bite, and then all start shouting at once that it was their idea.

choices.text: Share it with the whole table

effects.log: Twelve pieces of egg, very small. Everyone gets a piece. The cook monk shakes his head, and smiles in the way monks are not supposed to.

choices.text: Ask whose idea it was

effects.log: Everyone's, apparently. The little ones had saved the dye from the spring festival for months. You do not cry. You come very close.

events.text: Someone new arrives at the temple: a toddler in a basket, no name, no day. The other children look at you, the expert on birthdays.

choices.text: Help the little one choose a day

effects.log: You hold up two cards with the days written on: first snow, or the day the swallows come back. The toddler grabs swallows. It is a good day.

choices.text: Give the little one your own birthday to share

effects.log: Two eggs, dyed red, on the first snow. The toddler does not understand. You understand enough for both of you.

choices.text: Start the register of every child's chosen day

effects.log: You write it on the inside of the kitchen door: names, days. The abbot lets it stay. Generations of children add to it after you.

events.text: On the morning of your chosen birthday, a bundle is left at the temple gate with your name on it in an unfamiliar hand. Inside: a pair of padded winter shoes, exactly your size.

choices.text: Wear them at once

effects.log: They are warm and well-made, stitched by someone who knew how. You walk around the courtyard in them all day. The abbot, asked, says he saw nobody.

choices.text: Wait at the gate all night to see who brings things

effects.log: You fall asleep against the gatepost. In the morning there is a quilt over you that was not there before.

choices.text: Give them to a smaller child who needs them more

effects.log: The shoes are too big for the little one, who wears them anyway, clomping. Next year two pairs are left at the gate.

events.text: Every year, a bundle. Shoes, a jacket, a brush and ink, once a small carved wooden tiger. This year there is a note, in the same hand: 'You are growing well. Forgive me for not coming in.'

choices.text: Write a reply and leave it at the gate

effects.log: You write: 'Come in. I will not be angry.' In the morning the note is gone. Nobody comes in. But next year's bundle has a sweet in it, wrapped in red paper.

choices.text: Ask the abbot who it is

effects.log: The abbot is quiet for a long time. 'Someone who could not keep you, and could not forget you. That is all I know, and all I will say.' You accept this, nearly.

choices.text: Keep the notes in the wooden tiger's box

effects.log: You keep them all, every one. On bad nights you take them out and read the one line over and over.

events.text: This year no bundle comes. Instead the abbot gives you a small cloth pouch. 'Left with me in the spring,' the abbot says, 'by someone who was very ill. To give you when you were old enough.' Inside is a jade hairpin and a few words: 'This was your mother's. Be well.'

choices.text: Go to the gate and bow to the road

effects.log: You bow, once, very deep, to nobody, to the road. The abbot stands beside you and bows too.

choices.text: Keep the hairpin on you always

effects.log: It is plain green jade. It is the only thing you have from before. You never sell it, not in the hardest years, and it is a very long life.

choices.text: Ask the abbot to help you find out more

effects.log: The abbot helps. A name, a village, a grave on a hillside three days' walk away. Someday you will go there. Not yet. Knowing is enough for now.

events.text: Old Kong, who leads the beggars under the east bridge, says a beggar without a song is just a hungry person. Today you are to learn the bamboo clapper song: two bamboo slats, a rhythm, and a rhyme about the street you are on.

choices.text: Practise until your fingers blister

effects.log: Clack-clack, clack. By evening you can make the rhythm and Old Kong grunts approval, which is the highest praise there is under the east bridge.

choices.text: Make up your own rhyme

effects.log: Your rhyme is about the fat cook at the noodle shop. It is rude. It works. The fat cook throws a bun at you, laughing, which is the point.

choices.text: Ask why a song makes a difference

effects.log: 'Because a song is a gift,' says Old Kong. 'People pay for gifts. They only pity hunger, and pity is tight-fisted.'

events.text: Market day. A rich merchant's sedan chair stops at your corner, and the curtain lifts. The merchant has heard you are the child with the clapper. 'Sing me something about myself,' the merchant says. 'If I laugh, a silver bit.'

choices.text: Sing a rhyme about the merchant's belly

ok.log: The merchant laughs so hard the chair rocks and the bearers have to brace. A silver bit lands in your bowl. Old Kong, watching, nods.

fail.log: The merchant does not laugh. The curtain drops. The bearers laugh, though, all the way down the street.

choices.text: Sing a rhyme about the bearers instead

effects.log: The bearers grin. The merchant, who expected flattery, stares, then snorts. A copper, not silver. The bearers buy you a bun at the end of the day.

choices.text: Sing the old song Kong taught you

effects.log: Old, plain, sad. The merchant listens with the curtain up and gives you a copper without saying anything, and drives away.

events.text: Old Kong's voice is gone this winter, and the beggars under the east bridge sit in silence. Kong pushes the clappers into your hands.

choices.text: Sing for all of them, every day

effects.log: You walk the whole town every day with the clappers, and what you get you share under the bridge. Nobody under the east bridge starves that winter.

choices.text: Teach the little ones the song

effects.log: Six small clappers going at once, all out of time. People pay to make them stop, which is also a kind of payment. Old Kong laughs without a voice.

choices.text: Sing for Old Kong, under the bridge

effects.log: Just for Kong. The old songs, the rude rhymes, the sad one. Kong closes the old eyes and taps the rhythm on one knee.

events.text: At closing time, Auntie Hu the bun seller always has three or four buns left that are squashed or burnt on one side. She throws them to the dogs. One evening, she sees you watching the dogs.

choices.text: Ask for one

effects.log: She looks at you a long time. Then she gives you two, and says: 'Tomorrow. Same time. Do not tell the dogs.'

choices.text: Say nothing and wait

effects.log: She puts a bun on the step and goes inside, as if she had not seen you. You eat it on the step. Every evening after, there is a bun on the step.

choices.text: Offer to sweep her step for a bun

effects.log: You sweep it so clean she can see her face in it. She gives you three buns and a look that says she has not had an offer like that in years.

events.text: Two big boys from the river gang come to Auntie Hu's stall and take a whole tray of buns without paying, laughing. Auntie Hu shouts. Nobody in the street moves.

choices.text: Shout for the watch, loud

effects.log: Your voice is the loudest thing in the street. The watchmen come running, the boys drop the tray and flee. Auntie Hu picks up the buns, dusts them, and gives them all to you.

choices.text: Trip the second boy as he runs

effects.log: He goes down in the mud with an armful of buns. The street laughs at him. He will remember your face. You decide that is fine.

choices.text: Follow them to see where they go

effects.log: Under the west bridge. A gang of older children, and a very small one, sick, being fed the buns first. You go back and tell Auntie Hu. She is quiet for a long time.

events.text: Auntie Hu's wrists are sore, and the dough is heavy. She looks at you, grown taller, sitting on her step as you have every evening for years. 'You know the shape of a bun better than I do, by now,' she says.

choices.text: Learn to make the buns properly

effects.log: Up before dawn, flour to the elbows, the dough slapped and folded. Your first buns are rocks. Your fiftieth are buns. Auntie Hu pays you in buns and a corner to sleep in by the oven.

choices.text: Carry her trays to the market every morning

effects.log: Heavy trays, two at a time. Your shoulders grow broad. Auntie Hu sells twice as many with you shouting the prices.

choices.text: Give the burnt buns to the dogs yourself, now

effects.log: And to the river gang's small sick one, who is not sick any more. Auntie Hu watches you do it and says you are the stubbornest child she ever fed.

events.text: Under the east bridge the beggars sleep in a row on the dry stones above the water line. There is a rule: the oldest sleep furthest from the water. You are the youngest. You sleep with your feet nearly in the river.

choices.text: Accept the rule

effects.log: Old people's bones are cold. You understand that. Your feet are wet, but the old ones bless you in their sleep, and in the morning one of them shares a sweet potato.

choices.text: Build a little wall of stones to keep the water off

effects.log: It takes a week. Your corner is dry. The other young ones copy you. By summer the whole lower row is dry.

choices.text: Find a better place in the temple porch

effects.log: The temple porch is dry, but the monks wake you at dawn with a bell, and you miss the stories under the bridge. You go back.

events.text: The rains have been heavy upstream for a week. Tonight the river sounds different under the bridge: deeper, faster, a growl like an animal. The old ones are asleep. The water is already over your stones.

choices.text: Wake everyone and get them up the bank

effects.log: You shake every sleeper, shouting. Some curse you. They all come. An hour later the river fills the whole space under the bridge, roaring. Nobody says anything for a long time.

choices.text: Wake the oldest first, and carry their things

effects.log: You start with the furthest, the slowest, and the rest wake at the noise. When the water comes, everyone is on the bank and every bundle with them.

choices.text: Run for the watchmen

effects.log: The watchmen come with ropes and lanterns. It is chaotic and loud and everybody gets out, though two bundles are lost to the river.

events.text: After the flood the beggars move their sleeping place up the bank under the willows. Old Kong calls them all together and announces a new rule: the youngest no longer sleeps by the water. The one who hears the river does.

choices.text: Accept the job of listening to the river

effects.log: Every night you sleep lightly, one ear on the water. You learn the river's every mood. Nobody under the bridge is ever caught by it again.

choices.text: Teach everyone what the flood growl sounds like

effects.log: You make the noise, badly, and everyone laughs. But they all learn it. A river that warns, you tell them, is a kind river.

choices.text: Ask for nothing, and sleep under the willows like everyone

effects.log: Kong gives you the warmest spot anyway, without saying why. Everyone knows why.

events.text: For the first time your family takes you with the caravan to the western market: forty mules, bells, dust, and a camel driver from beyond the passes who speaks four languages and laughs at everything.

choices.text: Ride on the camel driver's camel

effects.log: The camel spits at you. The driver laughs. By the second day you can say 'water', 'thank you' and 'that camel is rude' in a language from beyond the passes.

choices.text: Count the mules every morning

effects.log: Forty. Forty. Thirty-nine. You raise the alarm. A mule is found in a melon field, eating. The caravan master gives you a copper and a job.

choices.text: Listen to the guards' stories at the fire

effects.log: Stories of sandstorms and bandits and a lost city in the desert. You do not sleep at all, and do not care.

events.text: Your second journey west. At the western market, spices are piled like mountains, horses with braided manes, a hundred languages. A trader with a beard dyed orange offers to swap you a little brass bell for the copper coin in your hand.

choices.text: Haggle in the trader's own language

ok.log: Three words from the camel driver, used right. The orange beard roars with laughter and gives you the bell AND the coin. 'A merchant already!'

fail.log: You say 'that camel is rude' by mistake. The trader laughs so hard the deal is forgotten, but you get a dried apricot for the joke.

choices.text: Ask your parent's advice

effects.log: Your parent looks at the bell, taps it, listens. 'Bad metal. See?' The note is flat. You keep your coin and learn to listen to brass.

choices.text: Trade fairly, coin for bell

effects.log: It is a cheap bell. It rings very sweetly. You tie it to your sleeve and are happy all the way home.

events.text: Years later the caravan comes back from the west without the camel driver, who has gone home beyond the passes. The caravan master brings you a small packet: a letter, in characters copied by someone else, and a carved camel.

choices.text: Have the letter read to you, then learn to read it yourself

effects.log: 'To the child who counted mules: you will be a great trader or a great nuisance.' You learn the foreign letters to read it yourself. It takes a year.

choices.text: Ring the brass bell on the caravan road

effects.log: You ride out with the next caravan, ringing the brass bell from the western market. The mules know it. They follow it like a song.

choices.text: Ask to travel with every caravan from now on

effects.log: Your parents look at each other. Then they agree. The road becomes your second home, and the world becomes larger every year.

events.arc: The Shop Cat and the Rat War
events.text: Rats have got into the family storehouse. The bags of rice are chewed. Your parents are furious. You, on the other hand, have found a small, filthy, one-eared cat in the alley.

choices.text: Bring the cat into the storehouse

effects.log: The cat sits in the middle of the floor and washes. The rats are unimpressed. So are your parents. You are not discouraged.

choices.text: Feed the cat first, then bring it in

effects.log: A fed cat, it turns out, is a patient cat. By the end of the week there are three dead rats on the storehouse step, arranged in a row, for you.

choices.text: Set traps yourself

effects.log: You catch a rat, two of your own fingers, and the shop steward's sleeve. The cat watches all of this with deep contempt.

events.arc: The Shop Cat and the Rat War
events.text: The one-eared cat has become a fat, glossy, one-eared cat called Abbot, who sleeps on the ledgers and is the most important member of the household. Today Abbot has gone missing.

choices.text: Search every warehouse on the street

effects.log: You find Abbot asleep on the silks in a rival merchant's shop. The rival merchant, astonishingly, asks to rent Abbot for a month.

choices.text: Shake the dried fish tin at the door

effects.log: Abbot appears from nowhere, as if summoned by magic, offended to have been worried about.

choices.text: Ask the street children to look

effects.log: Twelve children search the street, shouting 'Abbot!' Every monk in the temple comes out to see why. The cat is on the roof the whole time, watching.

events.arc: The Shop Cat and the Rat War
events.text: Abbot is old and slow now and the rats have noticed. Your parents say it is time to get a young cat. Abbot sits on the ledgers and looks at you with the one eye.

choices.text: Get a kitten, and let Abbot teach it

effects.log: The kitten is terrified of Abbot, who is terrifying. Within a month the kitten is a terror to rats. Abbot sleeps on the ledgers, retired, satisfied.

choices.text: Refuse: Abbot is still the shop cat

effects.log: You set traps yourself, every night, so that Abbot's record stays perfect. Abbot takes credit for every rat. You do not mind.

choices.text: Make Abbot a warm bed by the counting desk

effects.log: Abbot sleeps there, by the abacus, for the rest of a long life. Customers come in to stroke the famous one-eared cat. Sales improve.

events.text: The great family's spring banquet: forty tables in the main hall, every elder in silk. You have been seated at the children's table, far from the head of the house. A servant has made a mistake and put a cousin of a lesser branch beside you, who looks as if the floor might swallow them.

choices.text: Talk to the cousin as if nothing is wrong

effects.log: You talk about crickets. The cousin, slowly, starts to talk about crickets too. By the end of the banquet the two of you are the loudest table in the hall.

choices.text: Quietly tell a servant about the mistake

effects.log: The cousin is moved to the right table, red-faced but relieved. A watching elder notices how quietly you did it, and makes a note.

choices.text: Steal the best dumplings from the elders' table

effects.log: You crawl under three tables and come back with a plate. The cousin laughs so hard tea comes out of a nose. Nobody notices, except the head of the house, who says nothing.

events.text: At this year's banquet the head of the house sends for you. You must recite a poem to the guests, as all the children of the main line do. Every face in the hall turns to watch you climb onto the little platform.

choices.text: Recite the poem you were given

ok.log: Every line, clearly, in the old style. The guests nod. A visiting elder from another great family asks your name. The head of the house looks pleased, which is rare.

fail.log: You forget the third line, pause, and make one up. Some guests notice. The head of the house hides a smile behind a sleeve.

choices.text: Recite a poem you wrote yourself

effects.log: It is about a lesser cousin at the wrong table. The hall goes quiet. Some elders frown. The cousin, at the far table, is staring at you.

choices.text: Recite the shortest poem there is

effects.log: Four lines, twenty characters, about a well. Over in a breath. The guests laugh. The head of the house laughs too, which nobody has heard in a decade.

events.text: This spring the steward asks you to help with the seating of the banquet. Forty tables, a hundred quarrels, three branches of the family who must never sit within sight of each other.

choices.text: Seat everyone by rank, perfectly

effects.log: Not one elder is offended. The steward stares at your chart in admiration. The banquet passes with no incidents, which is a kind of triumph.

choices.text: Mix the branches at the children's tables

effects.log: The children of feuding branches sit together. Some fight. Most do not. Years later, some of the feuds end at weddings among them.

choices.text: Seat the lesser cousin at the main line's table

effects.log: Some elders mutter for a week. The cousin, at the high table, sits very straight and does not spill anything. The head of the house says nothing, which means yes.

events.text: Punishment, for breaking a window in the east courtyard: kneel in the ancestral hall until the incense burns down. Three hundred spirit tablets look down at you in the dark, rows and rows of gilded names.

choices.text: Read the names, one by one

effects.log: Three hundred names. A general, a scholar, a child who died at four. The incense burns down and you are still reading. The servant who comes to fetch you has to wait.

choices.text: Kneel properly and think about the window

effects.log: You kneel and think. The window was an accident. The lying afterwards was not. You go to the steward and say so. The steward is so surprised you are not punished again.

choices.text: Fall asleep against a pillar

effects.log: You wake at midnight in pitch dark, surrounded by your ancestors. You have never been so awake in your life.

events.text: Kneeling again (a different window). Behind the tablet of an ancestor six generations back, something pale: a folded paper, tucked in the gap between tablet and wall, thick with dust.

choices.text: Take it out and read it

effects.log: A letter, from that ancestor to whoever finds it: an apology, for a feud started over a horse, which the family has been fighting for six generations. The horse's name was Plum.

choices.text: Leave it where it is

effects.log: It is not yours to read. You kneel, thinking about it, until the incense burns down. You do not forget it.

choices.text: Tell the head of the house at once

effects.log: The head of the house comes with a lamp, reads it, sits down on the floor of the hall, and laughs until weeping. 'A horse. Six generations. Over a horse.'

events.text: The rival branch of the family, with whom the feud began, sends an envoy for the Qingming rites. Everyone is stiff and polite and furious. In your sleeve is the ancestor's letter.

choices.text: Give the letter to the rival envoy

effects.log: The envoy reads it in silence, then reads it again. Then the envoy laughs, the same helpless laugh as the head of your house. At the rites, the two branches bow to each other's ancestors.

choices.text: Bow to the rival branch's tablets first

effects.log: A child of the main line, bowing first. It is unheard of. The envoy is flustered and bows back, very deeply. The elders argue about it all week.

choices.text: Stay quiet and watch the elders

effects.log: The grown-ups circle each other like cats. You learn more about the family that day than in all your lessons.

events.arc: The Cousin Who Trains at Dawn
events.text: Every dawn, before even the servants are up, {npc}, a cousin of your own age, is already in the east courtyard practising the family's first form, over and over. The elders hold {npc} up as an example to you, constantly.

choices.text: Get up earlier than {npc}

mem.note: got up earlier than me to show off

effects.log: It is very cold at that hour. {npc} arrives to find you already sweating in the courtyard and is outraged. A war has begun.

choices.text: Watch {npc} from the gallery

effects.log: {npc} is good. Very good. And {npc} is crying, a little, between forms, where nobody should see. You go back to bed and think about it.

choices.text: Bring {npc} a hot bun at dawn

mem.note: brought me a bun at dawn

effects.log: {npc} is suspicious of the bun, then of you, then eats it very fast. 'Do not tell the elders.' You do not.

events.arc: The Cousin Who Trains at Dawn
events.text: The family's children's contest: the first form, before all the elders. {npc} and you are last, side by side. Everyone expects {npc} to win. {npc} expects it most of all, and looks ill.

choices.text: Do your best

mem.note: nearly beat me at the contest

ok.log: You are better than anyone expected. {npc} is better still, but only just. The elders mutter. {npc} looks at you differently from then on: a rival, not a nuisance.

mem.note: bowed to me at the contest

fail.log: {npc} is clearly better. You bow. {npc} is so relieved the form is over that {he} bows back, much too deep, and both of you nearly fall over.

choices.text: Whisper to {npc}: it is only a form

effects.log: {npc} breathes out. Does the form. It is the best {npc} has ever done it. You do yours well enough. Nobody else heard what you said.

choices.text: Make a deliberate mistake so {npc} wins

effects.log: {npc} wins. {npc} also saw you do it, and is furious with you for a month. Then, one day, says thank you, and is furious again.

events.arc: The Cousin Who Trains at Dawn
events.text: Dawn in the east courtyard. {npc} is there, as always. Today {npc} silently moves over to make room for you on the flagstones.

choices.text: Train side by side, every dawn

effects.log: No words. Just the first form, two of you, until the sun is up. The servants start calling the east courtyard the cousins' courtyard. Neither of you minds.

choices.text: Suggest you teach each other your weak points

effects.log: Your footwork, {npc}'s patience. A strange exchange. Both of you get better. Both of you would rather die than admit it to the elders.

choices.text: Challenge {npc} to a real spar

effects.log: A real spar, in the cold, until both of you are bruised and laughing. The elders, told of it, pretend to disapprove.

events.text: In the corner of the shed lies a heavy wooden board, cracked and blackened by fire, used as a table for drying mushrooms. Under the mushrooms, in faded gold, are four great characters. It is the old sect's signboard.

choices.text: Scrape the mushrooms off and read it

effects.log: Four characters, fire-blistered: the sect's name, the one nobody in the house says aloud. You trace them with a finger, one by one.

choices.text: Ask the family about it

effects.log: The answer is short and the silence afterwards is long. The old sect fell in a single night. Nobody uses the board as a table again after that question.

choices.text: Polish one character until it shines

effects.log: You pick the first character and polish it with ash and oil until the gold shows. One bright word on a black board. It looks like a star.

events.text: A stranger comes asking for the house of the fallen sect, and when shown the signboard, kneels in front of it in the mud. A former disciple, the stranger says. One of the last.

choices.text: Ask the stranger what the sect was like

effects.log: Halls on a mountain. Plum trees. Three hundred disciples who sang at dawn. The stranger talks until dark, and you listen until the fire goes out.

choices.text: Ask why the sect fell

effects.log: The stranger looks at you a long time. 'Betrayal,' the stranger says. 'And it was not your family's fault. Remember that, whatever anyone says.'

choices.text: Show the stranger the polished character

effects.log: The stranger touches it and laughs, and then does not laugh. 'That one. It means sincerity.' The stranger polishes the second one with you, all afternoon.

events.text: You have finished polishing the signboard, all four characters. It is too big for the shed. The family looks at it, gleaming, and at you.

choices.text: Hang it over the door of the house

effects.log: Neighbours stare. Some whisper. A few, very old, bow when they pass. The house has a name again, and you are its keeper.

choices.text: Wrap it in cloth and keep it until you can earn it

effects.log: You swear, quietly, alone in the shed, to hang it again one day over halls of your own. You do not tell anyone. The board knows.

choices.text: Ask the family what they want

effects.log: Your parent is silent for a long time. Then: 'Hang it inside. Where we can see it, and nobody else.' It hangs over the hearth for the rest of your childhood.

events.text: {npc} has lived in the back room since before you were born: a stooped old retainer of the fallen sect, who sweeps the yard and bows to your parents as if they were still masters of a mountain hall.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you to sweep like that

effects.log: {npc} sweeps in long slow arcs, the broom never lifting. 'Footwork,' {npc} says. 'All footwork is sweeping.' You do not understand. You sweep anyway.

choices.text: Bow back to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} stops dead, broom in hand. Then bows again, deeper. You bow deeper. It goes on until you both start laughing.

choices.text: Bring {npc} tea in the evenings

effects.log: {npc} drinks it slowly and tells you the names of the old sect's peaks, one per cup. There were nine.

events.text: In the yard at dawn {npc} is teaching you a breathing method that matches the sweeping: one breath per arc. It is the first method of the old sect, {npc} says, the one every disciple learned on the first day.

choices.text: Breathe with the broom

ok.log: Arc, breath, arc, breath. On the hundredth arc there is warmth under your navel, small as a coal. {npc} watches you and, for the first time, smiles.

fail.log: You lose the rhythm every time. {npc} says it took {him} two years. You keep going, and the broom wears a groove in the yard.

choices.text: Ask why {npc} stayed when everyone else left

effects.log: 'Someone had to sweep,' says {npc}. Then: 'And someone had to be here when the sect had a child again.' {npc} looks at you.

choices.text: Sweep the whole yard so {npc} can rest

effects.log: {npc} sits on the step and watches you sweep, and corrects your arcs with a word now and then. It is a sort of teaching. It is a sort of rest.

events.text: {npc} is dying, very quietly, in the back room. {He} asks for you. From under the mat {he} takes a small seal of carved stone, the old sect's seal, worn smooth, and puts it in your hand.

choices.text: Promise to keep the seal safe

effects.log: 'Not safe,' {npc} whispers. 'Used. One day.' {npc} dies that night, with the broom by the door. You sweep the yard at dawn, one breath per arc.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} until the end

mem.note: stayed with me at the end

effects.log: You hold {his} hand. {npc} tells you the names of the nine peaks once more, slower each time, and stops at the eighth. You say the ninth for {him}.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to name you a disciple of the sect

effects.log: {npc} laughs, very weakly, and says the old words, the ones from the first day. You are the last disciple of a sect that is gone, and the first of one that is not yet.

events.text: In the market you see a thin child stealing a radish, and your blood goes cold. You know that face. In your last life it was a grown face, and the murim called it the Butcher of the Western Road. Here it is a hungry child of six.

choices.text: Buy {npc} a bun

effects.log: {npc} stares at the bun, then at you, as if a bun from a stranger must be a trap. Then eats it in four bites and runs. The next day {npc} is back at the same corner, waiting.

choices.text: Watch {npc} from a distance

mem.note: stared at me in the market

effects.log: {npc} is just a child: dirty, quick, frightened of everyone. You remember what that child becomes. You cannot square the two.

choices.text: Tell the radish seller you will pay

effects.log: The radish seller lets go of {npc}'s collar. {npc} runs without a word, then stops at the corner and looks back at you for a long time.

events.text: {npc} follows you everywhere now, three steps behind, pretending not to. Today some bigger children are throwing stones at {npc} in the lane, and {npc}'s eyes have a look you have seen before, in the last life, on a grown face.

choices.text: Stand in front of {npc}

effects.log: A stone hits your shoulder. The big children hesitate. In the last life nobody stood in front of {npc}. You are fairly sure of that. They leave.

choices.text: Take {npc}'s hand and walk away

mem.note: walked me out of the lane

effects.log: You walk {npc} away from the lane. {npc}'s hand is shaking. {npc} says nothing, and does not let go until your gate.

choices.text: Tell {npc}: you do not have to become anything

mem.note: told me I did not have to become anything

effects.log: {npc} looks at you as if you were mad. But {npc} remembers it. Years later {npc} says it back to you, word for word.

events.text: {npc} has a place now: an apprentice at the tanner's, with a straw bed and three meals. {npc} comes to find you with the first coins {he} has ever earned, and tries to give them all to you.

choices.text: Take one coin, and tell {npc} to keep the rest

effects.log: {npc} keeps the rest, puzzled. In your last life this face was feared on every western road. In this one {npc} goes back to the tanner's whistling.

choices.text: Refuse them all, and say: buy someone a bun

mem.note: told me to buy someone a bun

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, then goes to the market and buys a bun for a thin child stealing a radish. You watch from the corner. Something in you, very old, lets go.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth about your last life

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down. 'Me? The Butcher?' {npc} does not believe a word. That, you decide, is the best possible ending.

events.text: You remember this summer. In your last life, in your twelfth year, the dam above the village broke in the seventh month. The memory is a cold stone in your stomach. Nobody else knows it is coming.

choices.text: Start piling stones on the high ground, every day

effects.log: The village thinks you are building a play fortress. You let them. By the twelfth year there is a wall of stones on the hill, chest high.

choices.text: Tell your family what you remember

effects.log: They laugh, then stop laughing when you describe the headman's dead mule, which has not died yet. They do not believe you. They are uneasy.

choices.text: Watch the dam, and wait

effects.log: You walk up to the dam every week and look at it. There is a crack near the sluice that nobody has noticed. You remember that crack.

events.text: The rains of the seventh month begin, exactly as you remember. The river is rising. The dam is groaning. The headman's mule has died. The grown-ups are uneasy, but nobody is moving, and you know which night it will go.

choices.text: Show the headman the crack in the dam

effects.log: The headman climbs the dam with you in the rain, sees the crack, and goes white. That night the whole village moves up the hill. At midnight the dam goes, exactly as before. This time the count on the hill is right.

choices.text: Lead the children up to your stone wall

effects.log: Twenty children up the hill, behind your play fortress. The parents come after them, angry, and stay, because at midnight the dam goes and the valley becomes a brown lake.

choices.text: Beg your family to go up the hill tonight

effects.log: Your parent looks at your face, sees something not childlike there, and goes. Others follow your family. When the dam breaks at midnight, most of the village is on the hill. Not all.

events.text: A year after the flood, the village has been rebuilt higher up the slope. At the shrine, in your last life, there were thirty-one names on a board. You go to look at the board in this one.

choices.text: Read the board

effects.log: The board is blank. A new one, freshly planed, with nothing written on it. You sit down on the shrine steps and shake, and do not know if you are laughing or crying.

choices.text: Help carry stones for the new houses

effects.log: You carry stones all summer. The headman calls you the child who saw the flood coming. You do not say how.

choices.text: Wonder what else you remember that you could change

effects.log: The flood was only the first thing. There are other memories in you, colder ones. You start, quietly, to make a list.

events.text: You remember holding a sword. You remember the weight, the balance, the cut. Your hands now are small and soft and cannot close properly around a chopstick.

choices.text: Practise with the chopstick anyway

effects.log: Draw, cut, return. With a chopstick. Your family thinks it is adorable. You are furious. You keep going.

choices.text: Wait. Bodies grow

effects.log: You make yourself wait. It is the hardest thing you have ever done, in either life. The waiting itself is a kind of training.

choices.text: Play like a child, and remember later

effects.log: You play in the mud. You chase the hens. You let yourself be small, for once. In the last life you were never small.

events.text: A neighbour's child is learning the village's clumsy fist form from a retired guard. Every move is wrong. Every move, you know from another life, will hurt the child's knees by thirty.

choices.text: Correct the child's stance, quietly

effects.log: You move a small foot one finger's width. The retired guard sees it and stares at you as if you had grown a second head.

choices.text: Say nothing; it is not your life

effects.log: You watch, and bite your tongue, and later the child's knees hurt anyway. You think about that for a long time.

choices.text: Ask the retired guard to teach you too, and learn it wrong on purpose

effects.log: You learn the wrong form perfectly and hide the right one under it. Nobody suspects a thing. You feel very old.

events.text: Your hands have grown. They close around a stick of firewood the way they once closed around a sword hilt, and for a moment the two lives overlap so exactly that you have to sit down.

choices.text: Pick up the stick and do the old form, all of it

effects.log: Twelve years of waiting in one form. When you finish, the yard is very quiet and a hen is staring at you.

choices.text: Put the stick down. This life can be different

effects.log: You put it down. You go and help with the washing. The old form is still there, folded in you, waiting. It can wait a bit more.

choices.text: Carve the stick into a sword, slowly

effects.log: A week of carving. The balance is exactly that of the sword you remember. You do not show it to anyone.

events.text: A fortune teller with one tooth and a bamboo tube of sticks sets up at the crossroads. Every child is told something grand: a general, a minister, a great beauty. You shake the tube. The stick says you will be a famous seller of dumplings.

choices.text: Refuse to accept it

effects.log: 'I will be a sword saint.' The fortune teller shrugs. 'Sword saints also eat dumplings.' You stamp home in a rage and practise with a stick until dark.

choices.text: Ask what kind of dumplings

effects.log: 'Pork and chive,' says the fortune teller, without hesitation. 'Very famous ones.' You decide that is not so bad, actually.

choices.text: Shake the tube again

effects.log: Same stick. You shake it a third time. Same stick. The fortune teller is starting to look uneasy too.

events.text: Everyone in the village has heard about the prophecy. Children call you Dumpling. The baker gives you a free bun 'for a future colleague'. You have had enough.

choices.text: Train harder than anyone, to prove it wrong

effects.log: Up before dawn, running the hill, punching the haystack. The village children stop calling you Dumpling and start calling you Mad Dumpling.

choices.text: Make dumplings, to prove you can and then stop

effects.log: Your first dumplings are a disaster. Your fifth batch is good. Your tenth is excellent. This is very alarming.

choices.text: Laugh along with them

effects.log: You call yourself Dumpling first, so the name has nothing to bite. By summer nobody calls you it except your friends, and they mean it kindly.

events.text: The fortune teller is back at the crossroads, older, with no teeth at all now. Children are shaking the tube. You wait in line, arms folded, to have it out.

choices.text: Demand a new fortune

effects.log: You shake the tube. The stick says: famous seller of dumplings. The fortune teller looks at the stick, at you, and starts to laugh helplessly. You start laughing too. You cannot help it.

choices.text: Ask how the sticks really work

effects.log: The old one looks around, then whispers: 'I tell every child something. The ones who fight it work hardest.' You stare. 'And the dumplings?' 'Ah. That one was real.'

choices.text: Bring the fortune teller a plate of your dumplings

effects.log: The old one eats one, then three, then the whole plate, and sits back. 'Well,' the old one says. 'I am never wrong.'

events.text: A wandering martial artist at the village inn calls for food. The cook is sick. Everyone in the kitchen looks at you.

choices.text: Make dumplings, pork and chive

effects.log: The martial artist eats forty. Then asks who made them, and comes out to the kitchen to bow. 'Strong wrists. Patient hands. You would make a fine swordsman.' You nearly drop the ladle.

choices.text: Say you are going to be a sword saint, not a cook

effects.log: The martial artist laughs. 'Then cook like one.' You make the dumplings. They are excellent. The prophecy, you decide, can share.

choices.text: Make them, and sell the rest at the crossroads

effects.log: By evening you have a queue. By the end of the month you have savings. The prophecy, it seems, is a fine thing to have in your pocket on the way to being a sword saint.

events.text: At the noodle stall by the bridge, a huge silent man pulls noodles: a lump of dough stretched, folded and slapped until it is a hundred threads, then a thousand. He never speaks. His arms are like temple pillars.

choices.text: Watch him every day after market

effects.log: Stretch, fold, slap. He never looks at you. On the tenth day he sets a bowl of noodles on the counter in front of you and goes back to work.

choices.text: Try it yourself with the dough scraps

effects.log: Your noodles snap, tangle, and land on the dog. The noodle-puller watches this, and his huge shoulders shake. He is laughing. Silently.

choices.text: Ask him why he never talks

effects.log: He points to his throat and shakes his head. Then he points at the dough and at your hands, and pushes a lump across the counter to you.

events.text: He has given you your own lump of dough. Every day he corrects you with his huge hands over yours: not pulling, he shows you, but letting the dough's own weight do the stretching. Softness, then a sudden snap of the wrists.

choices.text: Make your first real noodles

ok.log: Sixty-four threads, unbroken. He holds them up to the light, nods once, and drops them in the pot. You eat your own noodles, which are the best thing in the world.

fail.log: They snap at sixteen. He gives you another lump without any sign of impatience. You will come back tomorrow.

choices.text: Practise only the soft part until it is perfect

effects.log: Ten days of letting the dough fall. You begin to feel the moment when it wants to stretch and the moment when it wants to tear.

choices.text: Practise only the snap of the wrists

effects.log: Your wrists ache. The snap gets faster. A fly lands on the counter and you catch it without thinking. The noodle-puller raises his eyebrows very high.

events.text: Three toughs from the river gang knock over the noodle stall's bench and demand money. The noodle-puller wipes his hands on his apron and steps out from behind the counter. Something in the way he stands makes the toughs go quiet.

choices.text: Stay behind the counter, as his hand tells you

effects.log: You watch. Soft, then the sudden snap: three toughs land in the river, one after another, without a single blow you can actually see. He goes back to his dough.

choices.text: Run for the watchmen

effects.log: By the time the watchmen come, the toughs are sitting in the river, dazed, and the noodle-puller is serving a customer. The watchmen arrest the toughs, confused.

choices.text: Pick up the bench and set it right

effects.log: As you set the bench right, the toughs look at you and at him and decide the bridge is not worth it. He pats your head with a hand like a roof tile.

events.text: An old martial artist in a sect robe comes to the stall, stares at the noodle-puller, and goes pale. 'Iron Palm Gao,' the stranger whispers. 'We thought you were dead.' The noodle-puller goes on pulling noodles.

choices.text: Stand between them

effects.log: The stranger looks at the small child guarding a legend, and laughs in disbelief, and bows to you both. 'Then the legend is in good hands.' And goes.

choices.text: Ask the stranger what Iron Palm Gao did

effects.log: Thirty duels, unbeaten, then one terrible day nobody speaks of, and then nothing. The stranger leaves. The noodle-puller has heard every word and does not look up.

choices.text: Serve the stranger a bowl of noodles you pulled yourself

effects.log: The stranger eats, slowly. 'Soft, then the snap,' the stranger says. 'The Iron Palm's first lesson. In a noodle.' And looks at you very hard.

events.text: One morning the noodle stall is shut. On the counter is his rolling pin, worn smooth as jade, and a lump of dough under a damp cloth, still fresh. He has gone.

choices.text: Open the stall yourself

effects.log: You pull noodles at the bridge for a year. People come for them. Soft, then the snap. Your arms grow thick and your hands grow quiet.

choices.text: Practise the soft and the snap, every day, empty-handed

effects.log: No dough now. Just the arms, the softness, the sudden snap. One day you break a plank you did not mean to break, and stand there amazed.

choices.text: Keep the rolling pin, and his secret

effects.log: You never tell anyone who the noodle-puller was. The rolling pin hangs by your door for the rest of your life.

events.text: {npc} is the biggest child in the lane and takes everyone's lunch, every day, with a shove and a sneer. Today {npc} takes yours. You notice {npc} does not eat it.

choices.text: Follow {npc} after school

effects.log: {npc} goes to a shack behind the tannery and gives all the lunches to two small children and a coughing grandparent. You go home without saying anything.

choices.text: Shove back

effects.log: You both end up in the ditch. {npc} is much bigger. You get a black eye. {npc} gets a look of surprise that you will remember.

choices.text: Tell the teacher

effects.log: The teacher scolds {npc} in front of everyone. {npc} stands there red and silent, and that evening takes nobody's lunch, and you see {him} by the river looking at the water.

events.text: Lunch time. {npc} comes toward you with the usual shove ready. You are holding two lunches instead of one.

choices.text: Hold one out before {npc} can take it

effects.log: {npc} stops. Takes it slowly, as if it might bite. Neither of you says anything. The next day, {npc} does not take anyone's lunch, and you bring two again.

choices.text: Hide the second one and give {npc} nothing

effects.log: {npc} takes the first and finds the second. 'What is this?' You have no good answer. {npc} looks at you strangely and gives the second one back.

choices.text: Get the lane children to share too

effects.log: Everyone brings a little extra. It is collected, without a word, in a basket at the school door. {npc} picks it up every day, and nobody's lunch is taken again.

events.text: {npc}'s grandparent is very ill. {npc} is not at school. Someone has to fetch the doctor from the town, and the doctor has to be paid.

choices.text: Run to the town for the doctor

effects.log: Two hours each way. The doctor comes grumbling on a mule. You run alongside. The grandparent recovers. {npc} cannot look at you for a week.

choices.text: Empty your savings for the doctor's fee

effects.log: It is everything you had. {npc} finds out and tries to pay you back for a year, a copper at a time.

choices.text: Go and sit with {npc}

mem.note: sat with me by the door

effects.log: You sit by the shack door with {npc} all evening, not talking. Sometimes that is what is needed.

events.text: Some new bigger children are taking lunches from the little ones now. In the lane, {npc}, grown huge, steps in front of them.

choices.text: Stand beside {npc}

mem.note: stood beside me in the lane

effects.log: Two of you. The new bullies look at you both and decide to be somewhere else. {npc} grins at you, the first grin you have ever seen on that face.

choices.text: Let {npc} handle it, and watch

effects.log: {npc} does not hit anyone. {npc} says: 'Bring two lunches.' The new bullies have no idea what that means. You do.

choices.text: Find out why the new ones are hungry

effects.log: Same reasons. Always the same reasons. You and {npc} start a lunch basket again. It is still going years later.

events.arc: The Oath Under the Peach Tree
events.text: You, {npc}, and the tanner's child have heard the story of the three sworn brothers of the Peach Garden. Behind the temple there is a peach tree in blossom. You have a bowl of well water and three sticks for swords.

choices.text: Swear the oath: born on different days, to die on the same

mem.note: swore the peach oath with me

effects.log: You all say it, very seriously, and splash each other with the water. A monk watching from the gate pretends not to laugh. It is the most important thing you have ever done.

choices.text: Swear something smaller: to always share sweets

effects.log: 'That is not how the story goes,' says {npc}. 'It is how our story goes,' you say. The oath is sworn. It is kept better than most.

choices.text: Argue about who gets to be the eldest

effects.log: You argue until sunset. Nobody is the eldest. Somehow you are all sworn anyway, covered in petals, hoarse.

events.arc: The Oath Under the Peach Tree
events.text: The tanner's family is moving to the city. The third of your oath stands at the cart with a bundle, trying not to cry. {npc} is trying even harder.

choices.text: Give your stick sword as a keepsake

mem.note: saw the third off with me

effects.log: The tanner's child takes it, solemn. 'I will bring it back.' The cart goes. {npc} punches you very gently on the arm and you both go to sit under the peach tree.

choices.text: Promise to write

mem.note: promised to write to the third

effects.log: You cannot write very well. You promise anyway. {npc} promises to help you. The letters, when they come, are terrible and precious.

choices.text: Run after the cart all the way to the bridge

mem.note: ran after the cart with me

effects.log: You and {npc} run until the bridge, shouting. The tanner's child waves the whole way. At the bridge you stop, out of breath, and the world is suddenly bigger and lonelier.

events.arc: The Oath Under the Peach Tree
events.text: A letter from the city, in the tanner's child's crooked hand: the new street is loud, the new school is cruel, and could you both please come at the Spring Festival.

choices.text: Save up for the journey

mem.note: walked to the city with me

effects.log: A whole year of errands. At the Spring Festival you and {npc} walk two days to the city, and the three of you sit on a step in a strange street eating sesame cakes, and are complete.

choices.text: Write back every week instead

effects.log: Every week, a letter, from both of you, full of village news and bad jokes. The letters back get less sad, then funny. Distance, it turns out, can be crossed with ink.

choices.text: Send a peach blossom pressed in the letter

effects.log: The reply says only: 'I put it on my wall. Now my wall is the peach tree.' {npc} reads it three times and goes very quiet.

events.arc: The Oath Under the Peach Tree
events.text: At the peach tree behind the temple, after years, all three of you again: you, {npc} and the tanner's child, taller, voices cracking, the tanner's child carrying your old stick sword, wrapped in silk.

choices.text: Renew the oath, properly this time

effects.log: Same words, same bowl of water, same tree, older. The same monk watches from the gate, older too, and this time does not hide the smile.

choices.text: Laugh about the first time

mem.note: laughed under the peach tree with me

effects.log: You laugh about the splashing, the petals, the argument over the eldest. Some oaths do not need renewing. They just need remembering.

choices.text: Plant a new peach tree beside the old one

mem.note: planted a peach tree with me

effects.log: Three children with one spade. It takes all afternoon. Years from now, whoever swears an oath here will have two trees.

events.text: At the Lantern Festival the scholars' guild hangs riddles under the lanterns on slips of red paper. Guess one right and you win a sweet. Guess the great riddle on the biggest lantern and you win a brush of real wolf hair.

choices.text: Try every small riddle in the street

effects.log: You get eleven right and nine wrong. Your pockets are full of sweets. You will be sick tomorrow. It is worth it.

choices.text: Stare at the great riddle all night

effects.log: 'What has a mouth but never eats, a bed but never sleeps?' You stare until the lanterns burn down. You do not get it. You will.

choices.text: Make up a riddle for the scholars

effects.log: You write yours in charcoal on a scrap: 'What is small, and asks too many questions?' A scholar laughs and hangs it among the others.

events.text: Washing at the river at dawn, months later, it hits you all at once: a mouth but never eats, a bed but never sleeps. The river.

choices.text: Run to the scholars' guild to tell them

effects.log: The old scholar who wrote it laughs. 'Months late. But you did not give up.' There is no wolf-hair brush now. There is a cup of tea and a long conversation.

choices.text: Make up your own great riddle for next year

effects.log: It takes you all year. It is about a shadow. You are fiercely proud of it.

choices.text: Teach the trick of riddles to your friends

effects.log: Look for the double meaning. Think of the word itself, not the thing. By the next festival your whole lane is a menace to the scholars' sweet supply.

events.text: Lantern Festival. The scholars' guild has asked you, this year, to write the great riddle for the biggest lantern. Half the town will try it.

choices.text: Use the shadow riddle you have polished all year

effects.log: 'Follows you everywhere, but flees from the lamp.' Nobody guesses it for three hours. Then a small child does, and you give the child your own sweets.

choices.text: Write one so hard nobody will ever guess

effects.log: Nobody guesses it. The scholars are delighted and slightly annoyed. Years later people still argue about the answer, which you never tell.

choices.text: Write one that only a child could guess

effects.log: The grown-ups try for hours. A six-year-old guesses it at once and wins the brush. The scholars applaud the child, and you.

events.text: Deep winter. The lane children have a secret: you dig a pit in the snow by the threshing floor, light a little fire, and bury sweet potatoes in the embers. The trouble is the night watchman, who patrols with a lantern and a gong.

choices.text: Post a lookout while the potatoes cook

effects.log: You are the lookout. You see the lantern coming, whistle, and everyone hides behind the haystack, smelling of smoke and trying not to giggle.

choices.text: Cook them anyway, in plain sight

effects.log: The watchman's lantern swings toward you. Five children freeze. The watchman looks at the fire, at the sweet potatoes, and holds out a hand. It is the price of silence.

choices.text: Invite the watchman in the first place

effects.log: The watchman is so surprised to be invited to anything that he sits on the haystack and tells you ghost stories until the potatoes are done.

events.text: The night watchman is ill, and the lane is dark at night. Somebody has to walk with the lantern and the gong, or the town will think the lane is empty.

choices.text: Walk the lane yourself, striking the hours

effects.log: First watch, second watch. You strike the gong with great seriousness. The neighbours hear a small voice calling 'all is well' and smile in their beds.

choices.text: Bring the watchman sweet potatoes in bed

effects.log: He eats three, hot, and laughs about all the nights he caught you. 'You never fooled me once.' It is true. You are delighted anyway.

choices.text: Get all the lane children to walk it in turns

effects.log: A different child every night, very proud. The gong is struck at odd hours. Everyone is very safe and very tired.

events.text: The watchman, recovered, comes to the threshing floor with a basket of sweet potatoes and a bag of coal. 'For the pit,' he says. 'Fair is fair.'

choices.text: Cook them for every child in the lane

effects.log: Twenty children, one fire, one watchman telling the same ghost story he told you years ago. The little ones scream at the end. You remember screaming too.

choices.text: Ask him to teach you the watch

effects.log: The hours, the calls, how to walk and listen at the same time. Being awake while the world sleeps, you learn, is a kind of guarding.

choices.text: Give him the first and best potato

effects.log: He tosses it hand to hand, too hot to hold, laughing. 'You were always the polite one.' You were not. He remembers it that way.

events.text: After the first snow, there are footprints across the field behind the village. Each one is twice the length of a grown man's foot, and they are an impossible distance apart.

choices.text: Follow them

effects.log: They lead into the bamboo grove and stop, as if the walker stepped into the air. You go home in a state of tremendous excitement.

choices.text: Run and tell everyone there is a giant

effects.log: Half the village comes to look. The other half says you are making it up. Nobody can explain the stride.

choices.text: Measure the stride with a stick

effects.log: Five of your own steps between each one. You draw the pattern in the snow and stare at it. Whatever made them was not running. It was walking.

events.text: The giant footprints again, this time leading up to the hermit's hut on the ridge. Standing outside it, stretching, is a very small old hermit on a pair of very tall stilts.

choices.text: Laugh until you fall over

effects.log: The hermit laughs too, from far up. 'Every winter someone thinks there is a giant!' The hermit lets you try the stilts. You fall in the snow eleven times.

choices.text: Ask why the stilts

effects.log: 'Balance,' says the hermit, from a great height. 'If you can walk on these in snow, you can walk on anything.' The hermit hands you a smaller pair.

choices.text: Keep the secret from the village

effects.log: You never tell. Every winter the village argues about the giant. You keep a very straight face, every time.

events.text: The snow is deep. You stride across the field on your own stilts, each step twice a man's length, and stop at the bamboo grove, and step off onto the low branch, exactly as the hermit taught you.

choices.text: Leave giant prints for the village children to find

effects.log: The next morning, from the hermit's ridge, you watch the children come out and stare at the prints. One small child is measuring the stride with a stick.

choices.text: Walk to the hermit's hut and race

effects.log: Two pairs of stilts across the snow. The hermit wins by a stride and gloats for an hour. Your balance, you notice later, is better on everything.

choices.text: Practise standing on one stilt

effects.log: You stand on one stilt in the snow until the hermit comes out and gives you a long, thoughtful look. 'Who taught you that?' 'Nobody.' 'Hm.'

events.text: The old banyan by the shrine is hung with hundreds of red ribbons, each with a wish written on it. Climbing it to tie your own, high up, you can read the others. You should not. You do.

choices.text: Read them all

effects.log: A new roof. A cure for a cough. For a son to come home from the army. A puppy. For the river to stop flooding. You climb down slowly, carrying them all.

choices.text: Read only the ones on your branch

effects.log: One says, in a child's hand: 'I want one friend.' There is no name. There is a little drawing of a dog.

choices.text: Tie your wish and climb down without reading

effects.log: It is their business. The tree keeps their secrets. You feel very honourable, and a bit sorry.

events.text: You cannot stop thinking about the wishes. Some of them are small. Some of them you could grant, if nobody knew it was you.

choices.text: Grant the puppy wish

effects.log: A litter of puppies at the miller's. You find out whose ribbon it was by the handwriting on the school wall. One morning a small child finds a puppy at the gate with a red ribbon on its neck.

choices.text: Grant the one-friend wish

effects.log: You find the child by the drawing of the dog, a quiet one at the edge of every game. You sit next to that child for a week. Then a month. The wish is granted. So, it turns out, is one of yours.

choices.text: Grant the cough wish with herbs

effects.log: Licorice root and honey, left in a jar at an old man's door. His cough is better by the new moon. He tells the whole lane the tree answered him.

events.text: The village is talking. The tree is answering wishes. People come from the next valley to tie ribbons. The shrine keeper is delighted and baffled. Nobody knows it is you. Nearly nobody.

choices.text: Keep granting the small ones, secretly

effects.log: A mended basket, a lost hen found, a letter written for someone who cannot write. You become very good at not being seen.

choices.text: Tell the shrine keeper

effects.log: The shrine keeper laughs for a long time, then makes you tea. 'The tree has always had helpers. I was one, at your age.'

choices.text: Stop, before people expect too much

effects.log: You stop. Some of the wishes are too big for a child. Some are too big for anyone. You tie one more ribbon of your own: that they come true anyway.

events.text: High in the banyan, on your old branch, there is a new red ribbon. It says: 'Whoever you are, thank you. Now it is your turn to wish.' It is in the handwriting of the shrine keeper.

choices.text: Write your real wish, at last

effects.log: You write it and tie it and tell nobody. It is a very big wish. It is allowed to be.

choices.text: Write a thank you back

effects.log: Two ribbons side by side on one branch, thanking each other. People who climb up to read them laugh, and do not understand, and leave smiling.

choices.text: Leave the ribbon, and grant one more wish instead

effects.log: There is always one more. You find it, on a high branch: a new roof. It takes the whole lane a week, and you organise all of it.

events.text: The village teacher's spring test: whoever writes the Three Character Classic from memory without a mistake gets a new brush. {npc}, who sits beside you, whispers that {he} has not learned it, and asks you to tilt your paper.

choices.text: Tilt it

effects.log: {npc} copies. You both get brushes. The teacher looks at your two papers for a long time, with the identical mistake in the eleventh line.

choices.text: Refuse, and offer to teach {npc} after

effects.log: {npc} sulks and fails. That evening you sit together in the yard and go through it line by line. {npc} learns it in a week, furious and grateful.

choices.text: Write so badly that copying is useless

effects.log: You write the Classic in the worst hand of your life. {npc} cannot read a single character. You both fail. The teacher is baffled.

events.text: The teacher calls you to stay after class. On the desk are two old test papers, side by side, with the same mistake in the eleventh line.

choices.text: Confess everything

effects.log: The teacher nods slowly. 'And {npc}?' 'Knows it now. Properly.' The teacher looks at you a long time and puts the papers in the stove.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: The teacher waits. You wait. The teacher sighs and puts the papers away in a drawer, not the stove. You think about that drawer for years.

choices.text: Say it was you who copied, not {npc}

mem.note: took the blame for the test

effects.log: It is a lie, and a kind one. The teacher knows both. 'You are a bad liar and a good friend,' the teacher says. 'Learn to be only the second.'

choices.text: Ask what the teacher means

effects.log: The teacher shows you the papers. They are someone else's: two children from years ago. 'I keep them,' says the teacher, 'to see who notices.' You are not sure what lesson that is.

events.text: {npc} comes to find you, waving a paper: {he} has passed the county test, on {his} own, with the best marks in the village. 'Eleventh line,' {npc} says. 'I got it right.'

choices.text: Laugh until you cry

mem.note: laughed with me on the school step

effects.log: You both laugh, sitting on the school step, until the teacher comes out to see what the noise is, and laughs too.

choices.text: Say you knew {npc} could do it

effects.log: 'Liar,' says {npc}. 'Mostly,' you say. {npc} buys you a sesame cake with the prize money.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to help you with the hard lines now

effects.log: {npc} sits beside you and tilts {his} own paper toward you, grinning. You do not look. You learn it.

events.text: Old Granny Lu, who weaves, gives you a tray of silkworm eggs as small as sesame seeds. 'Feed them mulberry leaves, fresh, every day,' she says. 'Every day. They do not understand holidays.'

choices.text: Feed them every day, without fail

effects.log: The tray hisses with tiny jaws. You pick mulberry leaves in the rain, in the sun, on festival days. The worms grow as fat as your finger.

choices.text: Name every one of them

effects.log: There are two hundred. You get to forty before you start reusing names. There are six called General.

choices.text: Watch them eat

effects.log: The sound of two hundred worms eating is like soft rain on a roof. You fall asleep beside the tray, more than once.

events.text: A new spring, a new tray, and this time you see it to the end: the worms stop eating, climb into the straw and spin themselves into white cocoons. Granny Lu says the next step is to boil them, to unwind the silk. You stare at her.

choices.text: Let Granny Lu boil most, and keep ten to hatch

effects.log: Ten cocoons on your windowsill. In two weeks ten white moths come out, and lay eggs, and the whole thing begins again. Granny Lu calls you a silk farmer.

choices.text: Help with the boiling and reeling

effects.log: The thread comes off the cocoon in one long, impossibly fine strand. You have never seen anything so delicate come out of something so ordinary.

choices.text: Refuse, and set them all free

effects.log: Granny Lu sighs and lets you. A hundred and ninety moths flutter round the village for a week. They cannot fly far. It was not the clever choice. It felt right.

events.text: Granny Lu has woven something from your silk: a narrow sash, plain white, very fine. 'Your worms,' she says. 'Your leaves. Your rain.'

choices.text: Wear it always

effects.log: It is the finest thing you own. People touch it and ask where it came from. 'My worms,' you say, and they laugh, and you do not mind.

choices.text: Ask her to teach you to weave

effects.log: The loom is a maze. Your first cloth is a lumpy rag. She makes you weave it again until it is not.

choices.text: Give it to Granny Lu, who has nothing of her own

effects.log: She looks at it, and at you, and puts it on, and wears it every day. Next spring there is a new tray of eggs on your doorstep.

events.text: On the hillside a cowherd not much older than you plays a bamboo flute for the cattle. The cows walk toward the sound. When the tune changes, they lie down. It looks like magic.

choices.text: Ask to learn

effects.log: 'You cannot play until you can breathe,' the cowherd says, and shows you how to fill your belly and let the breath out slow as honey. You go dizzy. You keep at it.
