choices.text: Carve your own flute from bamboo

effects.log: It has the right number of holes in the wrong places. It sounds like a sick goose. The cows look at you with deep suspicion.

choices.text: Lie in the grass and listen

effects.log: The cowherd plays until the sun goes down. You lie in the grass with the cows, and you think you have never been so calm.

events.text: The cowherd teaches you three tunes: one to call, one to rest, one to go home. Today the herd has scattered across the hillside before a storm, and the cowherd's hands are shaking.

choices.text: Play the call tune

ok.log: Your notes are wobbly. The cows lift their heads, one by one, and come down the hill to you. The cowherd stares at you as if you were a sorcerer.

fail.log: You play the rest tune by mistake. Half the cows lie down in the rain. You and the cowherd fetch them one by one, soaked and laughing.

choices.text: Run and round them up on foot

effects.log: Up and down the hillside in the rain, waving your arms. Exhausted, muddy, every cow home. The flute was quicker. This was more honest.

choices.text: Steady the cowherd's hands and let them play

effects.log: You hold the cowherd's elbow until the shaking stops. The tune comes clear. The cows come home.

events.text: The cowherd is going away to be a soldier. On the hillside, the last evening, the old bamboo flute is put into your hands. 'They will need someone to play for them.'

choices.text: Promise to play every evening

effects.log: Every evening, at sunset, on the hill. The cows know it. The village knows it. Somewhere far away, you hope, a soldier hears it in a dream.

choices.text: Play the go-home tune for the cowherd

effects.log: The cowherd laughs, wipes an eye, and walks down the hill as the cows do: slowly, without looking back. It is the right tune.

choices.text: Ask for a new tune before they go

effects.log: The cowherd plays one you have never heard. 'For when I come back.' You learn it that evening, by heart, and do not play it again for years.

events.text: A soldier comes up the hill at sunset, thinner, with a limp, and stops at the top. You are playing. The cows lift their heads and look at the soldier, and then at you.

choices.text: Play the tune for when they came back

effects.log: The soldier sits down in the grass and does not say anything for a long time. Then takes out a new flute, a soldier's, and plays it with you.

choices.text: Hand back the old flute

effects.log: The soldier takes it, turns it over, and gives it back. 'It is yours now. It knows your breath.' You play the go-home tune, and the cows, and the soldier, go home.

choices.text: Play the call tune, so the herd comes to greet them

effects.log: Twenty cows come to the soldier and push their noses into the soldier's hands. The soldier laughs for the first time in years.

events.text: The old granary at the edge of the village has been empty for years, and everyone knows it is haunted: there are noises at night, and once a light. The lane children dare you to go in after dark.

choices.text: Go in with a lamp

effects.log: Inside, behind the old rice bins, on a straw bed: a thin old man in a faded soldier's jacket, sitting up very fast, more frightened than you are.

choices.text: Go in without a lamp, quietly

effects.log: In the dark you hear breathing and an old voice humming a marching song very softly. You back out, and your heart takes an hour to slow down.

choices.text: Refuse the dare

effects.log: The other children call you a coward. That night, from your window, you see a small light in the granary, and someone moving slowly, like an old person.

events.text: The ghost is an old soldier with nowhere to go, who came home from the northern wars to find the family gone. He asks you, very politely, not to tell anyone.

choices.text: Keep the secret and bring food

effects.log: Rice balls, a sweet potato, once a whole fish. He eats slowly and tells you about the north: the snow, the walls, the horses of the steppe. He never talks about the fighting.

choices.text: Tell the headman, to help him

effects.log: The headman comes, frowning, and goes away thoughtful. The next week the soldier has a bed in the temple and a job sweeping the shrine. He is not angry with you. Mostly relieved.

choices.text: Ask him to teach you to march

effects.log: He laughs, a rusty laugh, and teaches you to march in the dark between the rice bins: left, right, turn. Your feet learn it at once.

events.text: The lane children are planning to raid the haunted granary with sticks and firecrackers, to drive out the ghost. You hear about it the evening before.

choices.text: Warn the old soldier

effects.log: He packs his things into a bundle in silence. Then stops. 'Bring them in,' he says. 'One at a time.' You do. He tells them about the snow. Nobody brings a firecracker again.

choices.text: Join the raid and steer it the wrong way

effects.log: You lead the raid to the old mill instead, which is very frightening and full of owls. The granary is left in peace.

choices.text: Tell the children the truth

effects.log: Some do not believe you. Some come with you to see. By the end of the week, the haunted granary has a dozen small visitors bringing food, and the ghost has a lot of grandchildren.

events.text: The old soldier is gone. In the granary, on the straw bed, folded: the faded jacket, a tin cup, and a carved wooden horse of the northern steppe, small enough to fit in a palm.

choices.text: Keep the horse

effects.log: You keep it all your life. Sometimes, holding it, you hear the marching song, and your feet keep time.

choices.text: Bury the jacket under the granary floor

effects.log: A soldier should rest somewhere. You bury it with the cup and say the only prayer you know. The granary is never haunted again.

choices.text: Walk to the temple to ask where he went

effects.log: The monks say he left in the night, walking north. Home, perhaps. Or back to the snow, where he made sense. You hope it was home.

events.arc: The Stone-Skipper of the River Bend
events.text: Every child at the river bend skips stones. The record is seven bounces, held by the cooper's child, who brags about it constantly.

choices.text: Practise until dark

effects.log: Flat stone, low arm, a snap of the wrist. By dark: five bounces. Your arm aches. You are coming for that record.

choices.text: Search for the perfect stone

effects.log: You spend all day looking. You find it: flat, round, smooth as an egg. You decide it is too good to throw. You keep it in your pocket.

choices.text: Ask the cooper's child for the secret

effects.log: The cooper's child is so surprised to be asked that the secret is given away at once: throw it like you are angry with the water.

events.arc: The Stone-Skipper of the River Bend
events.text: Contest day at the river bend. The cooper's child gets seven, again, and turns to you with a grin. Everyone is watching.

choices.text: Throw

ok.log: One, two, three... nine. Nine bounces. The river bend goes silent, then explodes. The cooper's child stares at the water, then at you, and starts to laugh.

fail.log: Six. So close. The cooper's child claps you on the back. 'Next year.' It sounds like a promise and a threat.

choices.text: Throw the perfect stone

effects.log: It skips eleven times and sinks out of sight across the river. Everyone screams. You did not want to throw it. It was worth it.

choices.text: Let the cooper's child keep the record

effects.log: You throw a careful five and bow. The cooper's child, oddly, is disappointed. 'You were supposed to beat me.'

events.arc: The Stone-Skipper of the River Bend
events.text: A travelling monk stops at the river bend, picks up a stone, and without seeming to try, skips it all the way across the river, where it climbs the far bank and stops at the foot of a tree.

choices.text: Ask how

effects.log: 'Qi in the wrist,' says the monk. 'And no anger at the water.' The monk shows you how to breathe out with the throw. Your next stone skips twelve times. You fall over.

choices.text: Try to match it

effects.log: You throw until your arm is jelly. The monk sits and watches, nodding, and leaves without a word. Next morning your stones go further than they ever have.

choices.text: Bring the cooper's child to see it

effects.log: The two of you, old rivals, stand at the bank with your mouths open. Then you look at each other and start practising together.

events.text: On market day the family pig, a black sow named Marshal for her bad temper, escapes through the gate and goes down the main street at a dead run, scattering ducks.

choices.text: Chase her

effects.log: You chase Marshal through the cloth market, the noodle stalls and the temple courtyard. She is faster than you. She is faster than everyone. The whole town is laughing.

choices.text: Rattle her feed bucket

effects.log: Marshal stops dead in the middle of the street, turns, and trots back to you as if nothing had happened. Everyone claps. Marshal accepts the applause.

choices.text: Sit down and cry

effects.log: A kindly noodle seller brings Marshal back, holding a noodle in front of her nose. You stop crying. Marshal eats the noodle.

events.text: Marshal has become famous. She escapes every market day. Some people come to market just to see it. The noodle seller keeps a noodle ready.

choices.text: Train Marshal to come to a whistle

effects.log: It takes a whole season and a great many turnips. Now, on market day, you whistle and Marshal comes trotting back through the crowds. People throw coppers.

choices.text: Fix the gate properly

effects.log: You and your family mend the gate. Marshal glares at it for a week. Then she learns to lift the latch with her nose.

choices.text: Let her run; she loves it

effects.log: Marshal runs every market day, and you run behind, and the whole town shouts encouragement. You become very, very fast.

events.text: A rich farmer from the next county wants to buy Marshal, famous as she is, for a great deal of money. Your family looks at you.

choices.text: Say she is part of the family

effects.log: Your family agrees, after a long look. Marshal lives to be very old and very fat and escapes, for the last time, at fourteen, to lie down in the sun by the temple.

choices.text: Let her go to the farmer, who has a big field

effects.log: The farmer's field is huge. Marshal runs in it all day. You visit once and she comes running at your whistle across the whole field. You go home happy and sad.

choices.text: Ask the farmer how much Marshal is worth

effects.log: The farmer names a sum. Your family laughs, because it is the price of a house. Marshal, unbothered, eats the farmer's hat.

events.arc: The Monk Who Could Not Catch a Chicken
events.text: A young monk has come to the village temple for a few years of practice in lightness technique, and the abbot has set him a test: catch the temple's red rooster with bare hands. He has been trying for a week. The rooster is winning.

choices.text: Help him corner it

effects.log: Two of you, one rooster. The rooster escapes over both of you. The monk lies in the dust and laughs until he cries.

choices.text: Show him how farm children catch chickens

effects.log: Slowly. Never chase. Crouch, wait, scoop. The rooster is in his arms in a moment. He stares at it, then at you. 'Again,' he says. 'Show me again.'

choices.text: Watch his footwork

effects.log: He leaps, he twists, he lands on one foot on the well's rim. The rooster still gets away. But you have never seen a person move like that.

events.arc: The Monk Who Could Not Catch a Chicken
events.text: The young monk has noticed something. You never chase, and you never miss. He asks if he can practise with you.

choices.text: Teach him to wait

effects.log: You crouch together in the temple yard all morning. The rooster comes to peck at his sandal. He catches it. His face is like the sun coming up.

choices.text: Ask him to teach you his leaps in return

effects.log: A fair trade. He teaches you to land soft, to step without sound. You fall a lot. You stop falling.

choices.text: Race him to the rooster

effects.log: You both dive. The rooster, offended, flies onto the temple roof and stays there for the rest of the day, crowing in triumph.

events.arc: The Monk Who Could Not Catch a Chicken
events.text: The young monk is leaving to go back to his monastery on the mountain. At the temple gate he bows to you, the proper bow, the one he gives his masters.

choices.text: Bow back, properly

effects.log: You bow, as deep as you can. He smiles. 'You taught me the hardest lesson of my training. Patience from a child, with a rooster.'

choices.text: Give him the red rooster as a farewell gift

effects.log: The abbot laughs until he has to sit down. The young monk walks up the mountain road with a rooster under one arm. It never escapes him again.

choices.text: Ask him to come back one day

effects.log: He promises. Years later a grey-robed monk stops at the temple, and asks the abbot, very seriously, whether the rooster's grandson is still as difficult.

events.arc: The Paper Dragon in the Drought
events.text: No rain since spring. The fields are cracked. The village elders decide on the old rite: a paper dragon carried through the streets to call the rain. Every child wants to carry a piece. You are given the tail.

choices.text: Carry the tail with your whole heart

effects.log: You wave the tail so hard the paper scales rustle like water. The elders say a good tail makes the dragon believe. You do not know if the sky believes. You do.

choices.text: Ask why a dragon brings rain

effects.log: An elder tells you about the dragon kings who live in the clouds and the deep rivers. You look at the empty sky and try very hard to imagine one.

choices.text: Paint new scales on the tail first

effects.log: Blue and green, like the river. The elders say the tail has never looked so fine. The dragon goes out to the fields with a gleaming tail and a shabby head.

events.arc: The Paper Dragon in the Drought
events.text: The next summer the drought comes back, worse. The dragon goes round the fields three times. Still no rain. The elders are arguing. Some of the grown-ups are saying the rite is foolish and they should dig the old well deeper instead.

choices.text: Say: why not both?

effects.log: Everyone stops arguing and looks at you. Then half the village carries the dragon and half digs. By the end of the week there is water in the well, and the elders claim the dragon helped.

choices.text: Go with the diggers

effects.log: You carry baskets of earth up from the well until your shoulders are raw. On the fourth day the bottom goes dark and wet. Everyone cheers. You fall asleep in the basket.

choices.text: Carry the dragon tail alone, round the dry fields

effects.log: You walk the tail round the fields by yourself, all evening, singing the rain song. An old woman, watching, joins you. Then two more.

events.arc: The Paper Dragon in the Drought
events.text: In the night, the sound wakes you: rain on the roof tiles. The whole village is out in the street in their nightclothes, faces turned up, laughing.

choices.text: Dance in the rain with everyone

effects.log: You dance until you are soaked through. The paper dragon, hung in the temple, gets wet and droops. Nobody minds.

choices.text: Run to the fields to watch the cracks drink

effects.log: The cracked earth drinks and drinks, darkening, closing. You stand there in the rain until dawn, as if keeping watch for the fields.

choices.text: Run to the temple to save the paper dragon

effects.log: You bring the tail in out of the rain, and dry it by the stove. Next drought, the elders say, the same tail. And the same child.

events.text: Mistress Wen of the Plum Inn has lost a gold earring, a gift from her late husband. She has turned the inn upside down. She is accusing the new kitchen girl, who is crying in the yard.

choices.text: Search the inn yourself

effects.log: You look where grown-ups do not: under the hens, in the ash pit, inside the water dipper. Nothing. But in the ash pit there are crow feathers.

choices.text: Talk to the kitchen girl

effects.log: She did not take it. You believe her. She tells you Mistress Wen was feeding the crows on the roof that morning, as she always does.

choices.text: Tell Mistress Wen the kitchen girl is innocent

effects.log: Mistress Wen stares at you. 'Prove it.' You have no idea how. You promise to anyway.

events.text: A year on, the earring is still lost, and you still think about it. Then it comes to you: crows. Crows love shiny things. On the roof of the Plum Inn, wedged in the ridge tiles, there is a crow's cache: buttons, a thimble, broken glass.

choices.text: Climb up and search the cache

ok.log: Under a copper button: a small gold earring. Mistress Wen screams when she sees it, then hugs the kitchen girl, then you, then the earring.

fail.log: You slip on the tiles and land in the rain barrel. But you saw the earring glinting. The innkeeper's son fetches it with a ladder.

choices.text: Ask the grown-ups to bring a ladder

effects.log: The inn's handyman climbs up, grumbling, and comes down with the earring and a very angry crow on his hat.

choices.text: Bring the crows something shinier to trade

effects.log: You leave a polished brass button on the roof edge. In the morning the button is gone, and in the gutter, carefully, is a gold earring.

events.text: Since the earring, people bring you their mysteries: a missing goat, a stolen kite, a love letter with no name. Mistress Wen calls you the Magistrate of the Plum Inn.

choices.text: Solve the missing goat

effects.log: The goat is on the temple roof. Nobody knows how it got there. Everybody knows who found it.

choices.text: Solve the stolen kite

effects.log: The kite was not stolen. It was traded, by a little brother, for a frog. Justice is done. The frog is returned.

choices.text: Refuse the love letter: some mysteries are private

effects.log: Mistress Wen nods slowly. 'A good magistrate knows what not to find,' she says, and gives you a plum.

events.text: After the spring rain the paddy outside the house is full of frogs, and at night they sing so loud the shutters hum. You lie awake listening. One frog has a deeper voice than all the rest.

choices.text: Croak back at them

effects.log: You croak in the dark. The paddy goes quiet. Then, all together, the frogs croak back louder. You giggle until someone comes to see what is wrong.

choices.text: Count the croaks

effects.log: One, two, many. You do not know the numbers past ten yet. You invent new ones. The frogs do not mind.

choices.text: Listen for the deep one

effects.log: Every night you listen for the deep voice. It is always there, under the others, like a drum under flutes. You fall asleep to it.

events.text: Daylight, at the paddy edge, you find the deep-voiced one: a frog as big as both your fists, green and gold, sitting on a lotus pad as if it owned the field.

choices.text: Say hello, very politely

effects.log: It looks at you. It croaks once, the deep croak. You are sure it said hello back. You tell everyone. Nobody believes you except the oldest grandparent in the lane.

choices.text: Try to catch it

effects.log: It jumps, you jump, you both land in the paddy. It escapes. You are covered in mud from head to toe and laughing.

choices.text: Sit very still beside it

effects.log: You sit so still a dragonfly lands on your knee. The big frog stays. The two of you watch the paddy together until you are called for dinner.

events.text: This spring the paddy is quiet. They have drained it to plant a new field, and the frogs have moved to the ditch by the road, where carts go by.

choices.text: Dig a little pond in the corner of the yard

effects.log: With a spoon, a shovel and great determination. It fills with rain. In a week, a frog. In a month, a choir. Your family says they cannot sleep. You sleep beautifully.

choices.text: Carry the frogs from the ditch to the river, one by one

effects.log: Forty trips in your cupped hands. The deep-voiced one is the last, heavy and patient. At the river it sits on a stone and sings, deep, like a thank you.

choices.text: Ask the farmers to leave one corner wet

effects.log: The farmer laughs, then thinks about it, then leaves a corner. 'Frogs eat the pests,' he says, as if it was his own idea.

events.text: Your family's ox is old and huge and slow, and you are put on its back every morning to ride it to the field. It does not need guiding. It knows the way. It knows everything.

choices.text: Lie flat on its back and look at the sky

effects.log: The ox walks. The clouds go past. You learn more about patience on that broad warm back than anywhere else in your childhood.

choices.text: Talk to it all the way

effects.log: You tell it everything. It flicks one ear now and then. You decide this means it agrees.

choices.text: Bring it a turnip every morning

effects.log: It takes the turnip from your palm with lips like a soft old glove. It begins to wait for you at the gate.

events.text: The ox will not move. It is standing in the middle of the road to the field, legs planted, ears back, staring at the bridge. Your parent is losing patience.

choices.text: Trust the ox and look at the bridge

effects.log: You go and look. Under the bridge, the main beam is cracked through, ready to give. Your parent goes pale. The ox is given two turnips that night.

choices.text: Pull its rope as hard as you can

effects.log: It does not move an inch. You give up and sit in the road. An hour later the bridge's rotten beam gives way under a passing barrow of bricks.

choices.text: Sing to it

effects.log: It does not move, but its ears come forward. While you sing, your parent goes to check the bridge, and comes back very quiet.

events.text: The ox is very old now. It cannot pull the plough any more. There is talk in the family about the butcher, quietly, when they think you are not listening.

choices.text: Beg for it to be retired to the back field

effects.log: There is a long silence at dinner. Then your grandparent, unexpectedly, takes your side. The ox goes to the back field, to eat clover until it is ready.

choices.text: Offer to do its work yourself

effects.log: You cannot pull a plough. You try anyway. The family watches you strain at it in the field and, without a word, the ox is not sold.

choices.text: Spend every evening with it

effects.log: You sit with the old ox in the barn every evening, talking. Whatever is decided, it will have had that.

events.text: The old ox lies down in the clover in the back field one warm autumn day and does not get up. You sit beside its great head. Its breathing is slow and warm on your hand.

choices.text: Stay with it to the end

effects.log: The breathing gets slower. Its eye looks at you, calm, the way it looked at the road and the sky and the bridge. Then the eye is still. It knew everything. It knew you.

choices.text: Bring one last turnip

effects.log: It takes it, very slowly, with its soft old lips. That is the last thing it does.

choices.text: Ask the family to bury it in the back field

effects.log: They do, all of them, with spades, in the clover. You plant a turnip on the grave. Your grandparent says it is the most sensible grave marker there is.

events.text: In a summer storm, lightning splits the old jujube tree at the crossroads straight down the middle. In the morning half the village stands around it. The wood of a lightning-struck jujube, the elders say, keeps evil away.

choices.text: Take a splinter for yourself

effects.log: You pick a splinter the length of a finger, black on one side, gold on the other. You carry it everywhere. You feel braver. You are probably the same.

choices.text: Help the elders gather the wood fairly

effects.log: Every house gets a piece. You make sure the widow at the end of the lane gets the biggest. Nobody argues with a child who is that serious.

choices.text: Feel sorry for the tree

effects.log: You sit with the split tree all morning. It was older than anyone in the village. It is strange to be sad about a tree. You are.

events.text: The jujube tree is not dead. From the split stump, in spring, come green shoots, two of them, one on each side of the black scar.

choices.text: Water it every day

effects.log: You carry water up from the well every morning. The shoots grow as tall as you by the end of the summer. The village says the tree remembered you.

choices.text: Build a little fence around it

effects.log: Goats, children and carts are kept off. By autumn there are two thin trunks where there was one. Twins.

choices.text: Carve a charm from your splinter for the tree

effects.log: You hang it on the new shoots: a tiny jujube-wood charm, protecting a jujube tree. It makes the elders laugh, and then nod.

events.text: The twin jujube at the crossroads bears fruit for the first time since the lightning: small, red, wrinkled and sweet. The village children are lining up to see.

choices.text: Give the first fruit to the oldest person in the village

effects.log: The oldest grandmother in the village takes it with shaking hands. 'I ate from this tree at your age,' she says. 'And now again.'

choices.text: Plant the stones of the fruit all over the village

effects.log: Every corner, every ditch. In ten years there are jujube trees all over the village. Some people know why. Most just eat the fruit.

choices.text: Eat one yourself, sitting under it

effects.log: It is the sweetest fruit you have ever tasted. You sit under the twin trees with the black scar between them, and feel the storm and the spring at once.

events.text: Thunder rolls over the mountains, so loud the bowls rattle on the shelf. You are under the table. An old neighbour, Grandpa Bai, comes in out of the rain and crouches down to look at you.

choices.text: Stay under the table

effects.log: Grandpa Bai gets under the table too, with some difficulty. 'Thunder,' he says, 'is the sky moving its furniture.' You laugh, despite yourself.

choices.text: Grab Grandpa Bai's sleeve

effects.log: He lets you hold it. He tells you thunder is the drum of the Thunder Duke, who only punishes liars. 'Have you lied today?' 'No.' 'Then it is not for you.'

choices.text: Cover your ears and hum

effects.log: You hum until the storm is gone. Grandpa Bai hums with you, an old song, very badly. It helps more than anything ever has.

events.text: Another storm. Grandpa Bai takes you to the doorway, wrapped in a blanket, to watch. 'Count from the flash to the boom,' he says. 'Each count is a li away.'

choices.text: Count the storm coming in

effects.log: Ten. Seven. Four. One. The boom shakes your teeth. You do not hide. You are counting.

choices.text: Count the storm going away

effects.log: One. Three. Six. Ten. Twenty. You are delighted to see it go and almost sorry.

choices.text: Count and shout the numbers at the sky

effects.log: 'SEVEN!' The sky booms back. You shout louder. Grandpa Bai laughs until he has to sit down in the doorway.

events.text: A great storm, at night. Grandpa Bai is very old and very ill. He is lying in bed in his little house, and the thunder is shaking it. The neighbours say he is frightened.

choices.text: Go and sit with him and count

effects.log: You count, out loud, from flash to boom, until the storm goes. He falls asleep to your counting, the way you used to fall asleep to his.

choices.text: Tell him thunder is the sky moving its furniture

effects.log: He laughs, a thin laugh, and grabs your sleeve. 'Who told you that?' 'A liar,' you say. 'But it worked.'

choices.text: Hum his old song, badly

effects.log: You hum it as badly as he did. He hums along, worse. The storm passes. In the morning he is sitting up, and asks for rice.

events.text: Under the city gate, the letter writer sits at a little table writing letters for people who cannot write. Your handwriting has become good. The letter writer's eyes have not. One day you are asked to sit beside the table and help.

choices.text: Write exactly what people say

effects.log: A farmer's message to a son in the army, word for word: the pig is well, your mother is well, come home. It is the most important thing you have ever written.

choices.text: Help people find better words

effects.log: 'Say you miss him, not that the pig is well.' The farmer looks at you, startled, and agrees. The letter is better. The letter writer looks at you oddly.

choices.text: Ask why people cannot write

effects.log: 'Because there was no time, or no money, or no teacher,' says the letter writer. 'Not because they had nothing to say.' You look at the queue differently after that.

events.text: A woman comes every month to dictate a letter to her husband, a soldier at the northern wall. This month the letter that comes back from the north is in an unfamiliar hand, and she asks you to read it to her.

choices.text: Read it to her, gently

effects.log: It is from his captain. You read it slowly, as kindly as the words allow. She sits very still. Then she thanks you, and goes, and you sit very still too.

choices.text: Ask the letter writer to read it instead

effects.log: The letter writer reads it to her, and you hold her hand. It is the first time you understand that words can be heavier than anything.

choices.text: Write the reply for her, as she asks

effects.log: She dictates a letter to her husband anyway, to be burned at the shrine. You write every word. You burn it together.

events.text: The letter writer is retiring to a nephew's house in the country. The little table under the gate, the brush, the ink stone, the queue: they are looking at you.

choices.text: Take the table

effects.log: Every day under the gate. Letters to sons, to husbands, to creditors, to gods. You hear every kind of trouble, and every kind of love. You are never bored.

choices.text: Teach the people in the queue to write their own names

effects.log: One name at a time. Some of them cry when they first write it. The letter writer, told of it, says you are ruining a good business.

choices.text: Ask the letter writer to write you a letter, for once

effects.log: The old one writes it in a shaky hand, and you read it that night: 'For my best assistant, who writes what is meant, not only what is said.'

events.arc: The Day the Sun Was Eaten
events.text: At noon the light goes strange: thin and yellow, shadows sharp as knives. A bite has been taken out of the sun. The village is in an uproar. Everyone is banging pots to scare away the heavenly dog that is eating it.

choices.text: Bang the loudest pot you can find

effects.log: You bang the big wok with a ladle until your arms ache. The whole village is shouting. The sun keeps being eaten anyway. You bang harder.

choices.text: Look at the shadows under the trees

effects.log: Under the willow, the little spots of light on the ground are all crescents, thousands of tiny suns being eaten. You will never forget it.

choices.text: Hold the hand of a frightened little one

effects.log: The child is screaming. You hold the small hand and say the dog is very small and the sun is very big. It is not true. It helps.

events.arc: The Day the Sun Was Eaten
events.text: A year after the sun was eaten, the full moon rises the colour of rust. The village grabs its pots again. This time the old village teacher is standing in the square, looking up, perfectly calm.

choices.text: Stand beside the teacher and look

effects.log: 'The earth's shadow,' the teacher says quietly. 'Last year the moon walked in front of the sun. Tonight we walk in front of the moon.' You look up and suddenly it is not frightening, only enormous.

choices.text: Bang the wok again, for old times' sake

effects.log: One child banging a wok at a red moon. Then everyone. The moon comes back silver. The village cheers. You are very proud of your wok.

choices.text: Hold a frightened little one up to see it

effects.log: You lift the small one onto your hip. 'Look. It is only the moon blushing.' The little one stops crying and stares, and asks for it to happen again tomorrow.

events.arc: The Day the Sun Was Eaten
events.text: The calendar clerk from the county comes to ask what everyone saw. The elders talk about the heavenly dog. You put up your hand.

choices.text: Describe the crescents under the willow

effects.log: The clerk stops writing, looks up, and asks you to describe them again, slowly. Your crescents go into the county record.

choices.text: Say the moon walked in front of the sun

effects.log: The elders frown. The clerk smiles. 'That is what the old astronomers wrote. Who taught you that?' 'The teacher, under the red moon.'

choices.text: Say the wok banging worked

effects.log: The elders all agree loudly. The clerk writes it down with a very straight face. Children bang woks at the next eclipse too, in your honour.

events.text: A monkey trainer comes to the market with a small brown monkey in a red waistcoat that walks on stilts, beats a gong and passes round a bowl. While you are watching, it climbs down your arm and steals your sesame cake.

choices.text: Laugh and let it have the cake

effects.log: It sits on your shoulder to eat it, very politely, crumbs everywhere. The trainer says it has never done that before. The crowd gives twice as much.

choices.text: Snatch the cake back

effects.log: You and the monkey have a tug of war over the cake. The crowd roars. The monkey wins. It bows. You bow. Everybody throws coppers.

choices.text: Notice the chain on its ankle

effects.log: A thin chain, rubbed raw. You watch the monkey for the rest of the show and do not laugh at anything.

events.text: The monkey trainer is back, and drinking at the stall, and the monkey is tied to a post in the sun with no water. It recognises you. It holds out its little hand.

choices.text: Bring it water

effects.log: It drinks from your cupped hands, the whole bowl. The trainer sees and shouts, then sees the crowd watching, and starts giving the monkey water himself, very publicly.

choices.text: Tell the market headman

effects.log: The headman is not interested in monkeys. You are interested enough for two. You keep on until the headman, to get rid of you, orders the trainer to keep it in the shade.

choices.text: Untie it and let it run

effects.log: It runs straight up the temple tree and stays there all afternoon, gong in hand, while the trainer shouts. At sunset it comes down to you, not to the trainer.

events.text: The monkey trainer is gone from the market, and the old monkey has stayed behind, living in the temple tree. The monks feed it. It still wears the faded red waistcoat. It still steals sesame cakes, but only yours.

choices.text: Bring it a cake every market day

effects.log: Every market day, a cake, and the monkey on your shoulder, eating. The children think you are a sorcerer. The monks think you are a soft touch. Both are true.

choices.text: Take off the old waistcoat at last

effects.log: It lets you. Under the red cloth its fur is thin. In a month it has grown back, and the monkey looks like a monkey again, wild and glossy.

choices.text: Help the monks build it a shelter in the tree

effects.log: A little roof of bamboo in the fork of the branches. The monkey sleeps under it all winter and throws twigs at you in thanks.
